subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speechtext: The consideration of the proposed motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) for the Committee of Ways and Means, and the amendment of Mr. Turriff thereto, was resumed from Tuesday, May 8.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am reluctant to take any part in prolonging this debate, which, as I view it, has already become unwarrantably protracted. We are now in the third week of this discussion of the Budget, which, it seems to me, should have been disposed of in as many days. I believe that the people of this country have the conviction that we are spending a great deal of time in talking which could be better employed in doing. The times call for deeds rather than words. While of our best and bravest thousands are falling weekly in a great and noble cause, while the destinies of mankind are trembling in the balance, two hundred of us here are talking about matters that have no relation to the war, and are of the most trifling importance compared with the herculean task which calls upon us for our best and undivided attention. Questions by the hundred and motions by the score are placed upon the Order Paper, questions and motions that have no relation whatever to the war. I think it would be well to give the public a sample of a few of these questions and motions. I take one which was placed on the Order Paper on the 20th of April:
1.	How many permanent civil servants or officials were in the employ of the Department of Militia and Defence on the 10th day of October, 1911, and how many on the 31st of March, 1917?
2.	How many temporary civil servants and employees of all kinds were in the employ of the said Department on the 10th day of October, 1911, and how many on the 31st of March, 1917?
3.	How many permanent civil servants or officials were appointed by said Department since the 1st of August, 1914?
4.	How many temporary civil servants and employees were employed by said Department since August 1, 1914?
5.	What was the gross amount paid by said Department for salaries and expenses to both permanent and temporary civil servants and employees for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1914?

6.	What was the gross amount paid by said Department for salaries and expenses of all permanent and temporary civil servants and employees for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1917?
7.	How many civil servants were appointed by said Department since October 10, 1911, under the provisions of Section 21 of the Civil Service Act?
Seven questions in one. That is just one question qf thirty questions, in about the same words, that have been placed upon the Order Paper for each of the twenty departments of Government here at Ottawa. Here is another, a little shorter
May 1-1. What number of names has the National Service Commission received in answer to cards sent out?
2.	How many of these names are classified as military, agricultural, shipbuilding, and munitions prospects, respectively?
3.	How many are engaged in work that is regarded as non-essential in war time?
Here is another one:-
April 27-1. How many persons have been appointed to permanent positions on the Canadian Government railways from January 1, 1916, to March 31, 1917, who were not previously employed on the said railway?
2. What are their names, their salaries and the'positions to which they were appointed?
That question might have been amplified a .little and a little further information -elicited if the hon. gentleman who put it had asked whether each of these men bad hair on his head or not, and if so whether it was Ted or black. Here is another sample:-

of his successor,	_
That relates to ,a position of which the salary is insignificant, and the place concerned is an obscure hamlet. Here is another :-

I notice a new one to-day:-
1.	Who is the Indian agent of the Indian Reserve at Bear River, N.S.?
2.	When was he appointed, at what salary per year, and what are his duties?

13.	What were the names of Indian doctors on this reserve from October, 1911, to May, 1917, when were they appointed, and at what salary?
14.	If not on salary, what rate of pay dad they receive?
Just one more:-
1.	Has the Minister of Militia or any of the authorities of the Militia Department, official statistics as to the recruiting of soldiers in Canada for overseas service?
2,	If so, what are the correct figures of enlistments in the different overseas regiments raised since August, 1914, to date:	(a) Canadians speaking the French language,	(b)
Canadians speaking the English language and born in Canada; (c) British subjects by birth born outside of Canada; (d) British subjects by naturalization; (e) French Canadian soldiers in regiments commanded by officers speaking the English language raised in the Province of Quebec; and (f) French Canadian soldiers in battalions raised in the other provinces of Canada?
These questions, as I said, come in to us by the hundred, motions by the score, paralyzing the ordinary work of the clerks in the various departments, because it takes weeks, and in some cases months, to copy out all these vast returns, and perhaps it is not an exaggeration to say that in nine cases out of ten, after all this work has been performed, the returns are thrown into the waste basket

and this at a time when the destinies of mankind are trembling in the .balance. What has proportional representation or the reform o.f the Senate to do with the great war in which we are engaged? _ Yet we spent two days on those topics. Do 'hon. members realize that there are two hundred of us in this House, and that a day misspent-and we have had lots of them, talking about academic questions that have no relation whatever to the war-I ask do we realize that one day misspent means two hundred days' work of the 200 members of

this House lost to this country? Why, Mr. Speaker, a friendly stranger unfamiliar with party traditions, looking down upon us from the gallery, might he pardoned if he reached the erroneous conclusion that there are men more anxious to win the treasury benches than to win the war.
I would not at this stage say one word were it not that sneering references to and groundless accusations against the administration of the department over which I have the honour to preside have been made in this House. At this time, when the good offices of the department are sought daily from all directions, such vulgar sneers and false accusations only tend to frustrate the efforts so successfully exerted before, as since, the commencement of the war. Had such references and accusations and insinuations been limited to the hon. members for Eichmond (Mr. Kyte), Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles), and West Kent (Mr. MoCoig), I would not have paid the slightest attention to them. I would not have considered them worth noticing, because I believe that they would have no more influence without this House than they have within it. But when a member of the standing of the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), without cause or knowledge of the facts, so far forgets the dignity of his position as tp impute dishonesty and lack of integrity, I cannot permit him to escape without a protest, even at the expense of a little of the valuable time of this House. On many subjects the junior member for Halifax is well informed, and he is generally regarded as being as fair as the ethics and discipline f>f the Opposition permit. Certain it is that the hon. junior member for Halifax has not the faintest knowledge of the activities of tire Department of Labour and his guilt lies in indulging in wanton and ignoble criticism in profound ignorance of the facts. His legal training, anything like common fairness, and a reasonable regard for justice and for the rights of others, should have prompted him to seek the truth 'before making such sweeping and insulting imputations. Let me, Mr. Speaker, give the junior member for Halifax and his three or four partners in guilt a little light concerning the workings of the Labour Department.
During the last five years there has been no advertising branch in the Labpur Department. We choose rather to do our work as promptly, efficiently and unostentatiously as possible, leaving the results to
speak for themselves. I have no intent or desire to criticise adversely my predecessor in the .office which I have the honour to hold. He had and I have a most difficult task to perform, perhaps the most difficult and most trying of any department of the Government. I wish to show, therefore, by referring to some of the things that have been done in the Department of Labour, that we rather do things than advertise things. I repeat that but for these insulting imputations I would not have taken up a moment of the time of the House, because I do not think that such a course would have 'been justified.
What has been the record of the Labour Department during the last five years? Before I was placed in charge of the department some complaints had been made of alleged delays in establishing boards of conciliation after application had been received for such boards. I at once gave instructions that there should be no unnecessary delays, with the result that in the first year the average number of days elapsing between the receipt of application and the establishment of a board was reduced from 15 to 7. During the first year that I had the honour of presiding over the Labour Department we appointed several additional men known as fair wage officers-although their work has relation, to a very large extent, to matters other than that of fair wages. I was satisfied that it would be to the advantage of the Government and to the country if had a larger number of these men stationed at different points throughout Canada. In 1911 we had but two, whose headquarters were in Ottawa. Labour disturbances often come up suddenly, the first thing you hear of the trouble being a telegram saying: we are going to strike to-morrow. If, therefore, we had to send a man all the way from Ottawa to Vancouver or to Sydney to deal with trouble which had suddenly ai-isen, very serious difficulties might develop before he could reach the ground. I therefore sent a man- a very good man indeed-to Vancouver, which he has made his headquarters ever since. His work has been most satisfactory. He has been on the ground; he has been in a position to be aware of the first intimation of any labour trouble and to go at once to see the employers and the employees. It is no exaggeration to say that during the last five years his presence- there has prevented dozens of labour disturbances which would otherwise have developed in very serious manner. I appointed

quoted some figures as to prices in Australia. There are some conditions surrounding that which I think should be brought to the attention of the House: In the first place, when it is winter with us it is summer in Australia. We had a good crop in 1915; they had a very poor crop in 1915. We had a very poor crop and they had a good crop last year. There are seasonable prices; quite a large number of articles are cheaper in summer than they are in winter. I need not refer to anything beyond eggs. You can get eggs in the summer time for half the price that you pay in the winter and in January here, when we have midwinter, eggs are very dear. In January they have summer in Australia and then eggs are very cheap. But, when next winter comes around eggs are dearer there, Then again, in Australia they are unable at the present time to get their crop across the ocean to market. They are three times as far away from the market as we are, and they cannot ge_t tonnage to get their products there. I think that hon. gentlemen sitting behind me said the other night that there were 400,000 boxes of cheese at one place which they could not get away. They have millions of bushels of wheat which they cannot get across to the market. What is the result of all that?-a lowering of the price. They have a large quantity of products awaiting shipment, and the supply is greater than the demand-I mean demand that you can utilize, they being so far away from the market. Prices; rose more rapidly in Australia when they had a poor crop than they did in Canada when we had a good crop. That is very natural. Now, we have some figures. We have in our list 26 foodstuffs, 7 of which are meats. They have in their list in Australia 46 items of foodstuffs, 27 of which are meats. Meats were plentiful and cheap there when that list was made up. They were very dear here. It is almost impossible to make a just comparison between prices in Australia and in Canada.
I am going to take this opportunity of repeating what I have said before, because, perhaps, it will stand repeating. We have to-day, in all probability, 40,000,000 men under arms who have been withdrawn from productive work and who are now engaged in destructive work. It is said that as soldiers they consume about 50 per cent more than they would as civilians.. That means, if these figures are anyway near right, and they are only approximate, that
60.000.	000 are eating and producing nothing,
40.000.	000 of them fighting and destroying

everything in sight, human life as well as property. There are 60,000,000 consuming and 40,000,000 producing nothing and destroying wherever they go. Before this war broke out we did not have any foodstuffs to spare. Nobody thought of dumping shiploads of them into the ocean because we had more than humanity required. We had about enough to go around. Well, then, you remove 40,000,000 men, not all of them agriculturists, but a great many of them agri-. culturists, and employ them at destructive rather than productive work and the result is inevitable. In addition to that we had last year a shorter crop the world over than we had had for a great many years, a thousand million bushels of'wheat less last year than the year before. Millions of tons of food have been sent to the bottom of the ocean. What do we reasonably expect to result from all that-a falling off of 40,000,000 workmen consuming 50 per cent more than if they were civilians, and a short crop the world over? We felt it, perhaps, as much in the province of Ontario as anywhere else in the world, .because in many respects we had no crop at all last year outside of hay and fall wheat that grew on the higher land where it was not drowned out. Here you have, I submit, the great factors causing the rapid advance in the cost of foodstuffs. I admit there may be-and there is-some ground for holding that to a slight extent cold storage and combines, or something of that kind, may affect the prices, but to a very slight extent. That is something that we attempted to deal with by passing the Order in Council.
We did not pass it without consultation. We had amongst other delegations, quite a large number of the leading representatives of labour in this country, and they approved of an Order in Council such as we have here, or rather I think I should say they suggested it, and this Order in Council was passed. A good deal has been said about its inefficacy and the city of Montreal has been referred to. The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) read a large portion of a letter written by one of the officials of the city of Montreal, pointing out the impossibility of employing it to any advantage. If any hon. gentleman has read his letter he will notice that he devoted most of it to a discussion of the second part of the regulation. The regulation is as follows:
1. No person shall accumulate or shall withhold from sale any necessary of life beyond an amount thereof reasonably required for the use

or consumption of his household or for the ordinary purposes of his business;
2. Every person who shall at any time hold any necessary of life beyond an amount thereof reasonably required as aforesaid, and every person who shall hold, for the purpose of sale, whether as manufacturer, wholesaler, jobber, retailer or otherwise, any stock in trade of any necessary of life, shall offer for sale the said excess amount, or the said stock in trade, as the case may be, at prices not higher tl\an are reasonable and just.
Now, that official of the city of Montreal in dealing with that special provision- and that does not refer to any investigation by a municipality or by the Department of Labour, just with the question of the excess amount-left out these five words: "Or the said stock in trade," and he went on for half a column of newspaper space to show the impossibility of proving the excess amount over what he required for the ordinary operations of his business, leaving out altogether "or the said stock in trade." That is the main point of the regulation, the necessity of selling not only the excess but "the said stock in trade," and he is bound to sell it at a reasonable and just price. Thus when coal dealers, as mentioned by hon. gentlemen opposite, were selling coal at $6 a ton profit, that is selling it at $15 in the centre and $20 in the suburbs of the city of Montreal, any citizen of Montreal had a right to take action under that section, and under section 9 which provides:	.
Any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of these regulations shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable upon indictment or upon summary conviction under part 15 of the Criminal Code, to a penalty not exceeding $5,000, or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding two years, or to both fine and imprisonment as specified.
Any citizen of Montreal, knowing that -anyone refused to sell his stock in trade at a reasonable and just price, might have applied to the Attorney General of the province of Quebec for leave to prosecute, and if he could establish his charge in the police court of Montreal, the man guilty of violating that section would he liable to be fined $5,000 or to be sent to prison for two or three years. I think there is no getting away from that.

speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend from Glace Bay has mentioned this matter. I will come to that in a moment.
I was going to point out the course we took with reference, to Montreal. I noticed in the press one day that they were making these excessive charges for coal in Montreal. That was on the 27th of February, when the weather was pretty cold. I did not wait for an application from Montreal, from the mayor, or controllers, or the city council. I sent this telegram to the mayor of Montreal, off my own bat as it were:
I am informed that anthracite coal is selling in Montreal at from $12 to $15 per ton. There is no reason why price should be higher in Montreal than here where coal is selling at from $8.50 to $9.00 delivered. Is the information correct, and if so, has your municipality investigated conditions or applied for leave to prosecute any dealers charging unreasonable prices? I tender full support of this Department to any municipal action rendered necessary by the condition.
I received a reply from the mayor of Montreal the next day in these words:
You have been well informed. Anthracite coal is selling in Montreal as high as $20 a ton for delivery in the suburbs. In the centre of the city coal is selling as high as $15 a ton, and people have to beg to get it. The city of Montreal pays presently for coal $9 a ton taken in the yard. The city has done nothing up to now to put an end to this situation, and would welcome any suggestion you may make or any power the Government may give to prosecute those responsible for this state of affairs. If required I will send a municipal officer to meet you in Ottawa and discuss whole matter.
(Signed) MEDERIC MARTIN.
That was on the 28th of February. On the same day I sent a telegram to the mayor of Montreal:
Re anthracite coal situation. City has full investigating power and also power to cause prosecutions under existing regulations. I suggest that you send one of your city solicitors here to discuss means of improving Montreal situation.
He never sent any one. Now these regulations from which I read a moment ago contain a provision empowering the municipalities to make an investigation into matters within the boundary of their own municipality. We do not think that the Minister of Labour could undertake to>
make

We thought it would toe convenient to give the municipality power to investigate anything within its own 'boundaries. My hon. friend from Glace Bay, who is a lawyer, knows as -well as I do that, speaking generally, it is the duty of the provincial governments to enforce the criminal*laws' made by this Parliament. There are substantially no exceptions; there are two or three under the Customs Act and so on, but, speaking generally, there are no1 exceptions under our constitution. You would not think of writing to the Minister of Justice in Ottawa if somebody stole your horse; you would go to an officer of the provincial government, because it is the duty of the provincial government and of its Attorney General to see that these criminal laws are enforced. This is a quasi-criminal law. We give the municipality this power:
Whenever the council or any municipality shall declare by way of resolution that in its opinion excessive prices are being demanded within the limits of such municipality for any necessary of life, such council may, by notice in writing under the hand of its clerk or other authorized officer, require any person dealing within the municipality in such necessary of life, and locally situate therein, to make and render unto such council within a time set in such notice, and such person shall make and render unto such council, precisely as required by it, a written return under oath or affirmation, showing in detail-
(a)	The amount of such necessary of life held by such person for sale or disposition within such municipality at any indicated time or times including any time preceding the making of these regulations;

We have endeavoured to do something. We have prepared a set of regulations which are of great value. I do not mean to say that they are perfect. After an Act is passed by this Parliament and after we have attempted to administer it for any length of time, we find defects in it and we amend it, just as in the case of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act defects were revealed to my predecessor and defects have been revealed to me under our administration of it. That is our experience of administering the law. We pass an Act here for a certain purpose; we expect it to operate in a certain way; but we find, when we come to apply that Act, that it is defective. We come back to Parliament and ask that those defects be remedied. I do not contend that these regulations are perfect, but I do contend that two or three other gentlemen with myself have spent a long time in preparing them, and we did the very best we could. We shall be very glad to make any amendments that may be suggested'towards their perfection by my hon. friend from Glace Bay (Mr. Carroll) or by any other member in this House, or any one outside of this House. We are attempting to do something in the direction of helping the poor people.
The prices of the necessaries of life are very high, but owing to the fact that our working people aie employed throughout this country at high rates of wages, there is no suffering in this country. Our working pople, I am told, have more money than they ever had before. I do not say that is a reason why we should not do anything further for them in the way of a reduction in the prices of foodstuffs, but I say that the working people of this country are better off to-day than they have ever been before.. They are getting higher wages and many of them are putting money in the bank. I remember the time-I am only a boy yet-when the right hon. leader of the Opposition was a member of a government in this country, and when soup kitchens had to be opened and carried on in every great city and town in Canada to feed the people, and when the people went to the Government of which' my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition was a highly respected member, what were they told? The Government told them through its great Minister of Finance " The Government can do nothing. The Government

is merely a fly on the wheel. The only remedy is for the people to work harder and eat less." That is what the people were told at that time. Bnt we have made an effort to do something, and we have done something. I am satisfied that the publicity that has been given to these regulations has achieved something. We are administering them as well as we can; we have not had much experience in this particular line; we do not claim that they are perfect; we are ready to amend them if they can be improved. But we have done something by publicity. The wholesale men, the retail men and the consumers know that there are men in the Labour Department watching prices in the interests of the people of this country. The cards that come in set forth the exact truth, I believe, and where there is anything suspicious as to prices we get after them right away, and we propose to do so on every occasion.
With regard to Hamilton, let me repeat that we sent a capable man down there. I do not know what he did, as I have not had an opportunity of talking it over with him since; I have been so very busy looking afteT the hundreds of questions and scores of motions that hon. gentlemen opposite are putting every day. On account of our time being thus taken up, important 5 p.m. questions concerning this country are not receiving the attention they otherwise would. If hon. gentlemen opposite would drop these petty motions and questions and rise to the occasion it would be very much better. Let them follow the example of Elihu Root, or Teddy Roosevelt, and other leading men in the United States, who said to the President, " You are on the other side of politics, but that does not make any difference; we will stand behind you to a man; we will do everything that it is possible to do." Elihu Root said, " There is no coalition in the United States; we do not want any coalition; there is a coalition in every individual who is standing behind the President." If hon. gentlemen opposite would act in that way towards this Government we should have more time to look after prices in Hamilton and in the little town of Sarnia, in the constituency of my hon. friend from Lambton.

I regret that I was not here to listen to the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) make his statement, and to hear the reply of the critic (Mr. A. K. Maclean) on this side of the House. I have read the two speeches with some interest, and I may say that the reading of the Finance Minister's speech was a mingled joy and sorrow. I rejoice that we have been able to secure the necessary money to do our part in this great war. I rejoice that so many of our men had voluntarily taken their lives in their hands for the defence of home and liberty. I rejoice because of their heroic achievements. I rejoice that it is my privilege to make this statement on the floor of this House. But I sorrow, at the same time, because the Government has not been able to implement its undertaking to have 500,000 men in training or at the front. I regret that we seem to be unable to do our full part. I sorrow for the bereaved relatives of our fallen and maimed heroes. I sorrow because we lose their help in the development of this great country of ours. I make this further remark, and I make it entirely as a personal remark- the Government has tried in vain to fulfil its promises; but they are responsible for this failure and ought now, even now, to call others to their aid and, together with the Opposition party, form a government that would get the men, voluntarily or otherwise. If there were more unanimity of action, the complement of men would probably be forthcoming.
We learn from the Budget speech also that $60,000,000 of this fiscal year's receipts are available for war expenditures over and above the expenditures on consolidated revenue and capital accounts, including interest and pensions. It is interesting to me, and I suppose it will be interesting to other hon. members and the public at large, to know the sources from which the money expended during 1917 came. I may not have all the items, but I think the statement I shall make is practically correct. We find that fox the fiscal year ended March 31, 1917, war taxes were collected through the Customs amounting to $38,000,000. About $1,000,000 vas collected through the Inland Revenue Department in bill stamps

and other stamps on medicines, etc., and about $6,000,000 on spirits and tobacco- that is, in excess of what would have been collected under the rates of duty in existence before war was declared. Then, we collected about $6,000,000 in extra stamps through the Post Office Department. Besides there is $15,000,000 business tax. According to the Minister of Finance we had $60,000,000 to apply to war expenditure. But the figures I have given show that we have received from the people no less than $64,000,000 for war taxes paid in support of this glorious cause. I am glad to be able to congratulate the people upon the fact that, though so many other calls were made upon us, it was possible to raise this great sum by the contributions of rich and poor alike. This $64,000,000, divided among the families of Canada, and assuming five members -to each family, means that the average family in Canada paid as a war tax last year no less than $40. That, to my mind, is greatly to the credit of our people. But it is not to be forgotten that, while we collected through the Customs $38,000,000 of war tax, we collected also the fabulous sum of $110,000,000 which was used to defray the ordinary expenses of departmental administration, public works, and interest. That $110,000,000, divided amongst all the families in Canada, as I have already indicated, would mean a further tax on eviery family of not less than $75. [DOT] I repeat I am glad the Canadian people have the means of paying such taxation and thus helping to win the cause for which we are fighting and which is so dear to us. It has been well said that silver 'bullets will win the war. When the war started that statement was made by the present Prime Minister of England, then Chancellor of the Exchequer. Thus, it is important that we do our part not only in regard to men and munitions, tout in regard to money, because silver bullets are perhaps as much required for the winning of the war as are men and munitions.
The Government have increased the customs taxation, as they say, for a worthy cause, and I am not finding any fault with it in that respect. They have increased the tariff by five per cent on British goods and seven and a half per cent on importations from foreign countries. That means that while $84 on a given value was levied in 1915, $100 is being levied in the fiscal year 1916-17. The Government, in doing this, *were within their rights and they had the good will of the Opposition, but there was 
this difference between the Government and the Opposition: the Opposition thought it was unwise that the products of the Mother Country should thus be hindered from coming into this part of the Empire. They accept responsibility before the country for the stand which they have taken in regard to this matter, and they say that some other means should have been found for raising this extra money, rather than the imposition of an increased duty on commodities coming from the Mother Country to Canada.
There is another tiling regarding customs taxation that should, be home in mind. I have told you what the taxes are, that we have paid the equivalent of about $115 per family into the treasury by way of customs duties. But we ought not to forget that only about 25 per cent of the goods consumed in Canada are imported from abroad. The other 75 per cent is represented by our own Canadian manufactured goods. What I allege is that, while we consume Canadian goods, we pay -I will not say the whole-but a very large portion of the duty that would be collected if these goods were imported. We pay in duties which go into the treasury, together with whiat we pay the manufacturers because of the tariff, perhaps $300 or $400 per family annually. Thus we have in this country a tax so much of which is paid to the manufacturers and so much directly to the treasury. I think our slogan at the present time should be: reduction in the cost of food products, with lower tariff on imported food products, especially those not indigenous to' Canadian climate and soil.

Yes, cheaper fish, if it is possible to get it by reducing the duties on fish. I will stand by my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) on that doctrine. Take the duties off fish, take the duties off all natural products and reduce the duties on food products, even if they are manufactured in Canada, to the lowest minimum consistent with the necessary expenditure of the country. I think that is sound doctrine. I think the country will prosper under a tariff along those lines very much more than it will under a tariff the basis of which is what I call class legislation. I think the party "who put that class legislation tariff on the statute book are responsible for a good deal of the trouble that we have in this country. We stand for a tariff that does not imply or include class legislation.

With regard to the Budget speech of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), I have really not a word to say against the proposals he made. Very many of them, I realize, are necessary under the circumstances. The minister put it to the people of Canada how the'extra revenue wias to he raised. He indicated several sources of further taxation. He gave Tea-sons why it was not, perhaps, wise to impose higher taxation on luxuries, and I agree with a good deal that the Finance Minister said. With regard to the increased taxation on business profits, I do not see how he could very well do any better under the circumstances. Therefore, I have very little criticism to make in that regard.
Now I come to another matter, and I regret that I cannot speak in the same terms with regard to this. I think I might as well take up the criticism of the Finance Minister first. I had the pleasure of listening to the Minister of Finance while he addressed the House on the amendment which was proposed, and I regret to say that it was a heated, partisan speech that he made, so much so that I wondered if -an election was in sight next week or in ten days. The first passage in the minister's address to which I wish to refer is to be found on page 982. The Finance Minister was speaking of the right -hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and he used these words:-
My right hon. freind notwithstanding his free trade professions in 1S93, when he got into office followed in the footsteps of Sir John Macdonald and Sir Leonard Tilley-
- and so on. The reference to 1893 is to the Liberal platform which was laid down that year. I want to read another clause from the minister's speech. This is also in reply to ,a remark by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The remark was:

speechtext:
My hon. friend was
out of the House when I pointed out that among other reasons why my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) signally failed in 1911, was that he attempted to prove to the intelligent people of this country that the farmer would get more for his product and the consumer would pay less.
Do you notice that this is a pet phrase. There is not one word different, except that and " is substituted for " hut." He told my hon. friend:
My hon. friend would hardly expect me to embark upon that undertaking after the example of 1911.
The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lai or) spoke somewhat along the same lines. At page 1152 of Hansard he said:
It is the same old thing to-day as it was in the time of the reciprocity campaign, an attempt to deceive the people of this country. In my county on the day of the official nomination we always have a big public meeting in order that the candidates may express their views to the electorate. I remember that at the last official nomination during the reciprocity campaign a friend of mine handed me a leading Liberal paper of Toronto. One edition of that paper was issued for the farmers to read and the other for the people in the towns and cities. One told the farmers that if they had reciprocity they would get higher prices, that everything wuuld be worth more, butter, eggs, wheat, stocks of all kinds1-everything would go up. The other edition told the people living in the cities and towns that they would buy everything cheaper. Well, it was amusing.
I shall not attempt tp answer in detail the allegations of the hon. member for Haldimand. I should like, in the first place, to see the Liberal newspaper that made the statement in the words as there presented to the public through Hansard. I venture to say this, that the words are not accurate. I might enlarge on my reasons for thinking they are not accurate but I shall not do sc now. But if they are accurate, they are only the opinion of an individual writer, and not the opinion of the Liberal party as a party, nor are they the findings of the present leader of the' Opposition the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. But I think I .ought to reply to the allegation of the Minister of Finance. The words to which I want particularly to address myself are:
That the farmer would get more for his product and the consumer would pay less.
I want to tell the House, if I can, what is involved in that statement. In the first place, the statement on its merits, using

the exact words as there presented to the country and to the House, are. not accurate so far as the policy of the Liberal party is concerned; and they are not accurate as a statement of what was' involved in the reciprocal trade relations that were under the consideration of the country at that time. I wonder if the first allegation of the minister is correct. It is divided into two parts, that the farmer would get more for his product is the first statement.
I ask myself that question and I ask you that question, is it true that, under the reciprocal trade relations the farmer would get more for his product? Do I need a witness after the speech of the Minister of Finance? I have his testimony for it, be-oause he was so pronounced that it would be most unfair eight, five, or four weeks before, to have free wheat passed as part of the Budget. Why, he said, there were possibly 50,000,000 bushels in the West, and, at 10 cents a bushel, it would be $5,000,000, or if there were only 25,000,000 bushels, it would be, at 10 cents a bushel, $2,500,000. What about the $2,500,000? Why, he said, it would be just that much out of the pockets of the farmer in the West. Do I need another argument to buttress my case that the farmer does get the benefit of natural products going free into the American market, and that if his product is subject to duty, the farmer pays the duty?
If this is true regarding wheat, it is equally true regarding such products as fish, hay, potatoes, shingles, laths and so on, commodifies which were mentioned in the proposed reciprocal trade arrangement with the United States. Do I need any other argument than this to prove that the allegation of the leader of the Opposition and of the Liberal party is correct: that under the proposed trade arrangement, the producer of natual products in Canada, having the American market free, would get the benefit?
I see the Minister of Trade and Commerce before me. Would he say that the Canadian consumer would, under reciprocal trade arrangements with the United States, pay less for the products that he purchased? My hon. friend, for whom I have the greatest respect, would, no doubt, say in reply to that question: You had better be a little more definite; you had better not tease me by asking me something to whi'dh either "yes" or "no" would be a correct answer.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: He says that it is taken out of the realm of trade now.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
That is a pet phrase, if I may so express myself, of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because you will notice that, with the use of the word "and" instead of "but," he repeats it later in his speech. Half a truth is the very worst kind of misrepresentation; the very worst kind of lie. I say that that statement made by the Minister of Finance on behalf of the Tory party is a deliberate, wilful misrepresentation of the facts as presented to the people of Canada during the election of 1911. At that time I stumped my county from one end to the other, and I made no *such statement as that, leaving it where the minister left it. I made the matter clear, as I shall make it clear to this House in a few moments; yet the Tory press came out with head limes something like this: Heads I win, and tails you lose. Let me paraphrase that statement of the Minister of Finance and give it as my right hon. leader made it and as the intelligent people of Canada understand it:
The farmer would get more for his product and the consumer would pay less for United States products imported under the reciprocal trade arrangement from the United States.
It is true that under the reciprocal trade arrangement with the United States the farmer would get more for his products, and it is equally true that the consumer, buying American products coming into Canada free or under a reduced tariff, would get those commodities for less money.
The question was asked, in a local paper in my district, how I could argue that the United States consumers would not get the benefit of duties taken off goods entering the United States, whereas Canadian consumers would get the benefit of duties taken off goods entering Canada. This is true, and I will tell you why. On general principles, the country that imposes taxes on imported goods simply asks the consuming public to pay that tax. But there are exceptions to all rules; let me tell you that this is an exception to the general rule. First, it must be remembered that we have to the south of us a population of 100,000,000, in round numbers, and we have in Canada 8,000,000 people. When we buy a commodity in the American market, we must buy it at its market value in the United States, because we are not a sufficient factor materially to change the price. The United States market is a world market, and we must buy at their market price, or not buy at all. Let us examine the conditions of out selling in the United States such commodities as I have named. When

I was running my election, I contended that I was not sure that hard wheat would receive any benefit if the United States took the duty off, because I considered that the price on the Liverpool market largely determined the market value of wheat in the United States. Of course, I had reference to hard wheat. Now we have the minister saying that on low grade wheat the farmer will receive an additional 10 cents a bushel by Teason of the removal of the duty. As I say, if we market goods in the United States, we must accept the conditions that exist there. If I have no other market for, say, 10 carloads of fish, I must send them to the New York market and accept the New York market price. If the weather is cold and if fish are scarce, I get a better price, and whatever the duty is, I get that much less for the commodity that I market. That is true of potatoes, shingles, laths, hay, and of practically every commodity that was mentioned in the reciprocity trade arrangement.
If we were having an election at this time and if this statement of my hon. friend were made on a public platform, I would not mind it so very much, but I say it is unfair criticism for a minister of the Crown to repeat it in this House, using this slogan: " The farmer gets more and the consumer less," which on the fact of it is ridiculous. With a proper and true interpretation it is absolutely the case that on our home products that we would market under the reciprocal trade relation, the increased price would inure to the benefit of the farmers of Canada, and on the imported goods that would be .marketed under the same trade relation, the reduced duties would inure to the benefit of the Canadian consumers. How much benefit would the Canadian 'consumer receive? On the basis of the imports for 1910, the reduction in the duties would amount to $2,200,000; that is, under the reciprocal trade relation, the Canadian consumers would have paid $2,200,000 less than he actually had to pay for those imports in 1910. That is not all. I do not need to remind the Minister of Trade and Commerce of this fact, because I know that his mind is acute on these matters, even if he is not a practical business man, but let me remind other hon. members of it. The Canadian consumers pay $2,200,000 into the customs house of Canada, but do they pay more than that? In the first place the goods, after having been taken out of customs, are received by the wholesale merchant who adds on a 82
profit of not less than fifteen or twenty per cent. The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor), speaking about the Dominion Canners Limited, the other night, said that .they sold their goods at a profit of ten per cent, and the hon. member was quite correct in that statement, but he did not tell the whole story. Up to a certain point, they do sell their goods at an advance of ten per cent, but that is when they are delivered practically from the factory to the retailer without being taken into the wholesale warehouse, but for later delivery the price is raised 24 cents. That, however, is a digression. The point I wish to make is this, that the saving to the Canadian consumers would be practically $3,000,000, because the wholesale distributor adds fifteen or twenty per cent profit on to the $2,200,000 and then the retail merchant adds his percentage of profit on to what he has paid to the wholesale merchant. Therefore, I say that if we had had this trade arrangement for the last four years, the consumers of Canada would havie saved no less a sum than $12,000,000. There is, of course, a reasonable answer to my statement, namely, that in these war times we must have money and the treasury would be minus that amount if the reciprocal trade relations were in force. That would be perfectly true, but what I think is right is that the .country ought to know that these allegations of the Tory party are absolutely unfounded.
I wish to refer io just one more matter in regard to the reciprocal trade relation, because the Minister of Finance was again very partisan in regard to it. On page 983 of Hansard of this year, the minister said:
The chief objection was the fact of the agreement. It is true that on its face it was stated that it was not a treaty but in substance and in fact it was a treaty and when it was entered into the late Government lost to a considerable degree the control of its own tariff.
I do not consider that to be a fair criticism. I will read the words of the agreement and I will leave it to any hon,. member that listens to my voice to judge if that i6 a fair criticism of the words of the agreement. That is .the kind of criticism that helped to win the election of 1911, and it looks to me as if it will be used again as a slogan. No contract can be broken without the consent of both parties unless there is a clause in it empowering either party to break or change it, and that is exactly what is in this agreement, the words of which are as follows:



Nevertheless, it is distinctly understood that we do not attempt to bind for the future the action of the United States Congress or the Parliament of Canada, but that each of these authorities shall be absolutely free to make any change of tariff policy or of any other matter covered by the present arrangement that may be deemed expedient.
That means that after the agreement has been passed by Parliament, Parliament, on any occasion, the next day if they choose, can amend it. Ajoeording to the words of the contract they can do anything they please regarding what they have done. What more can you do to-day regarding wheat that you have put on the free list? You put it on to-day and you can take it off tomorrow. The power that made wheat free can unmake it. The power that made that agreement can unmake it, according to its terms. I may he dense; I may not understand the situation; I may not have the acute mind that the Minister of Finance has, but I fail to come to any other conclusion from the reading of the words of that agreement. I do not kn<w that I can say anything further regarding the Finance Minister's .address to the House or the amendment before the House.
I was surprised at the heated argument he made. He talked just as if an election were coming on next week, and "free wheat" was to be the slogan of his party; and incidentally they would ridicule reciprocal trade relations just as they ridiculed them in 1911. Suppose I were to ask the Minister of Finance: "Do you realize that you have taken out of the pockets of the farmers of Western Canada from $6,000,000 to $10,000,000 during the last three years?" I am sure that if he were in his seat he would say: ("Why how have I taken $6,000,000 or $10,0000,000 out of their pockets)" Let me answer him in his own words.	[DOT]

The words of the Minister of Finance to which I referred ate to be found in part on page 988, as follows :-
Well, ten cents on fifty million bushels means $5,000,000, and on twenty-five million bushels, $2,500,000. Does my hon. friend mean to say that if this is a proper course for us to take in the national interest at this time of war conditions, the farmer in the West is not entitled to that ten cents.

That is a question put by the minister to a member on this side of the House. Later -page 989-he said:-
They say we should have included this free wheat measure in the Budget, and debated it for a month or six weeks, and two months from now the proposals would be enacted into law. Supposing we had done that? It would mean that the farmer of the West would have been deprived all that time of ten cents a bushel in respect of the low grade wheat he exported to the United States.
Thus we have the testimony of the Minister of Finance, that, if there be 25,000,000 bushels of wheat in the West to-day for export to the United States, the removal of the duty will mean that the farmers will put $2,500,000 in their pockets. If the farmers of the West will be $2,500,000 better off because we put wheat on the free list at a certain time instead of two months later, how much better off would they be if wheat had been put on the free list in 1914? It is fair to say that the party in power to-day has deliberately and without good reason taken from the pockets of the farmers of the West a sum of not less than $6,000,000 to $10,000,000, and this with practically no benefit to any industry in Canada and no advantage to the treasury of Canada, the whole sum accruing to the benefit of the treasury of the United States, according to the testimony of the Minister of Finance himself.

speechtext: I thought I had made myself clear enough for the hon. gentleman to grasp the situation. If the farmer gets more for his wheat, and if that wheat is converted into flour and sold in Canada that flour is worth just that much more to the consumer. No argument can be used against this, except that it will be alleged that this affects adversely the Canadian miller. But do you mean to tell me that the millers of Canada, are not able to compete with the millers of any other country? We can export our wheat to all the markets of the world. Will anybody tell us, then, that we cannot compete in supplying our own market-that we cannot feed our own people? Do you mean to say that we need a bounty, or that our people must be compelled to pay more for flour than that flour is worth when we send it abroad? speechtext:
That is very kind of the hon. gentleman. If I had explained it to him that two and two make four, I suppose he would have "accepted" it as the best I could do, but would really be dissatisfied because I had not said that two and two make five.
Now, I wish to deal a little more at length with a statement of the Minister of Finance to which I have already referred.
The minister made the allegation that in 1893 the right hon. gentleman who leads His Majesty's loyal Opposition, laid down
a platform of free trade. And, the hon. member for Prontenac (Mr. Edwards), speaking the other evening, said:
Nor have I any particular regard or admiration for a leader who denounced protection as a thing accursed of God and man, and promised free trade, and yet for all the time he remained in power maintained that so called curse in practically the same position as it was when he assumed the reins of office.
That is a rather serious charge that the hon. member for Erontenac has made and perhaps there is not another hon. gentleman in this House who would make such an allegation as that. Let us see if that was the platform of the Leader of the Opposition in 1893. I was a delegate to the Liberal Convention of 1893. It was held in Ottawa three years before the general election of 1896. I had the pleasure of attending every one of those meetings. I heard the right hon. gentleman address the convention, I heard the speakers from different portions of the Dominion, and I say here and now to every hon. gentleman in this House that it is absolutely beyond the truth to tell the House that the policy of the Liberal party in 1893 was free trade. Such a statement can only he made with malice aforethought. If hon. gentlemen consult the minutes of the convention, they will find no such words in the platform of the Liberal party as laid down in 1893. It is unfair criticism for a Minister of the Crown to insinuate that the policy of the Liberal party in 1893 was free trade. It was on that platform that the Liberals went to the country. What was the platform of the Liberal party at that date? I need not tell hon. gentlemen because I am doubtful if there is any one in this House who does not know what that platform was. That platform was a tariff for revenue purposes and reciprocal trade relations with the United States in natural products. The .latter part of the platform was favoured by the Conservative party, 'and it had been their platform from the time of the abrogation of the old treaty. When hon. gentlemen send such innuendos as that across the floor of the House there must he something doing. I leave them to conjecture what it is. Now, Mr. Speaker, I would expect you to ask: have the Liberals carried out that platform? We have the innuendo from the other side of the House that we have not done so. I am not going to say that it was carried out in full. Perhaps it was not, but this was done and it oan be demonstrated by the blue book: In 1881, as a result of Sir John Maedonald's ministry

which, went into effect in 1879, as you will see by the Trade and Navigation Report issued by the Department of Customs in 1916, the average rate of duty was 20 09 per cent on dutiable and free goods. This means that two years after the Conservative tariff came into force 20-19 per cent was collected on imports dutiable and free. The Liberals came into power in 1896 and the Fielding tariff was adopted in 1897. In 1899, or two years after the Fielding tariff came into force, 16-17 per cent was collected on all goods dutiable and free, or 3-49 per cent less on the value of invoices for home consumption, or equal to about 17 per cent reduction in the amount of duty collected. On a given value, under the tariff of 1879, $100 was 'collected, while on the same amount in 1899, under the Fielding tariff, only $83 was collected.

While we did very materially reduce the rate of duty and made the tariff practically a revenue tariff, it is to be regretted that here and there in that tariff we find that class legislation of which I spoke this afternoon, protection for a certain interest at the expense of the public. I would say first of all that in this country a moderately high tariff seems to be a necessity. We have a large expenditure, and a moderately high tariff, based on proper principles, on principles of fair play to everybody affected, is perhaps something we cannot do without. We cannot dp without it at the present time, at any rate, nor can we avoid it unless something happens in the future which we can not now foresee. But I dO' say this, that it is unfair to tax the consuming public, say 40 per cent, on a food commodity, because that 40 per cent means 60 per cent when it reaches the consumer. I say it is most unfair to do that, and if blunders have been made in the past, hon. gentlemen opposite ought to rise to the occasion and correct the blunders. In these days when we are talking about high prices, the high cost of living, it is an opportune time for bringing food commodities down to a proper rate of duty. Of course we have the war expenditures to meet, and it may be that at the moment it is not opportune to effect this reform. But the principle that ought to be laid down in Canada today is the principle of the Liberal party, tariff for revenue purposes; and I say this, that in normal times, under ordinary conditions, no item of food product ought to be taxed under the tariff at over 20 per cent. I said, and I repeat, that a tariff for revenue purposes involves more or less protection.
It is incidentally a protection to every maker of the same kind of commodity. Moreover, if the maker of a 'commodity cannot, with a protection of from 20 to 25 per cent, compete with the maker of a similar commodity in another country he ought to divert his energies to some other field of activity. I do not believe in the doctrine of unduly taxing any commodity at the expense of the whole people; I believe that is not treating the people fairly. I pointed out this afternoon that perhaps every family in Canada is paying 3300 or 3400 a year into the treasury, or to the manufacturers of Canada, and I say that we should reduce that taxation as far as it is practicable to do so.
The hon. member for Halddmand (Mr. Lalor) made some reference to the Dominion Canners Company the other night. I have not a word to say as to how the business of the Dominion Canners Company is conducted or as to what prices they charge to wholesale grocers or to the consuming public. That is their own business, and it does not fall to me to criticise them. But it is up to the Government to see that the Dominion Canners Company charge the consuming public a proper price for their products. Let me illustrate what I mean. There were imported into Canada during the fiscal year 1916 about $222,000 worth of canned fruits. What duty do you suppose went into the treasury because of that import? No less a sum than $87,000. In other words, the Dominion CanneTS Company are protected to the extent of 40 per cent on the canned fruits that they put on the market. I refer to the report of the Department of Customs, page 106, in which I find these figures:
Fruits in air-tight cans or other air-tight packages, imports, general tariff, $222,940; duty collected, $87,672.06.
Thus, under the present tariff, the Dominion Canners Company are protected to the extent of practically 40 per cent, which, I say, is costing the consumers of Canada not only the 40 per cent, but the amount of the distributor's profit thereon-another 20 per cent.

The hon. member for Haldimand further said that every dollar of the capital of the Dominion Canners Company had been paid in hard cash. Wihat I would like to know is whether the hon. gentleman meant the preferred stock only, or the common stock as well. I venture to say that the hon. gentleman told only half the story. I presume that he had reference to the preferred stock only and that the common stock when it was distributed, was gratuitous. That means that if the Dominion Canners Company earned more than a reasonable dividend on the preferred stock, the common stock would get a dividend at the expense of the consuming public, whereas no actual cash may have been paid for that common stock. Let me say that if the Government would take the matter in hand, I would not be a bit afraid of improper or undue prices for canned goods. I would not care whether the Dominion Canners owned every factory in Canada, provided the Government would see that they are not protected beyond a reasonable duty. In 1915 there was a very large crop in Canada. There were in that year several independent factories and there was a large pack. Among the factories there was undue competition and fairly low prices prevailed. This is what happened, and this is what the Government should guard against:	What I
would call a holding company was formed, and the small canners came in under the Dominion Canners Company. Can you not understand, then, why they had a good year in 1916? The Government was at their back with a 40 per cent duty on fruits-it is not so much on vegetables. I am sorry that the hon. member for Haldimand is not here. I would not even hint at anything which I knew to be inaccurate, and if I have said anything that is incorrect it will give me a good deal of pleasure to withdraw it, and I shall endeavour to withdraw it as publicly as I have stated it.
I have incidentally referred to the speech of the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). I never in my life heard a more bitter or more partisan speech than I heard from the lips of that hon. gentleman the other night. I have read one of his statements; I wish to read a few more lines of what he said. I do not think that another gentleman in this House would make the assertions that were made by the hon. member for Frontenac. Listen to these words, Mr. Speaker. Take them under consideration as I read them.

I do not believe they represent the sentiments of the electors of Frontenac; I do not believe there is another gentleman in this House that would utter them. Listen to these .words:
A minister of the Crown seeks to impress upon the audience the importance of their duty in regard to the war, and he is hooted and jeered at and howled down by young men in that audience who evidently do not wish to listen to any appeals along the lines of recruiting or enlistment. The reason for this, Mr. Speaker, is clear. The man who is responsible for the condition of affairs that exists in the province of Quebec is the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition.
And further on the hon. member says:
His teachings, more than any other cause, are responsible for conditions prevailing to-day in the province of Quebec

and sad conditions they are.
What can I say to remarks of that character? They are without truth in fact; they contain an innuendo that ill becomes the strongest party man in the Tory party in Canada, for, if Sir Wilfrid Laurier has done any one thing more than another in Canada, it has been to cement the races rather than to cause division. When we came to Parliament in 1914 and the leader of the Government made known the sad conditions of war, the leader of the opposition voluntarily and promptly made the statement that he would uphold the hands of the leader of the Government in everything regarding the war, and since that time he has practised what he has preached. Yet the hon. gentleman from Frontenac has the audacity to throw that innuendo across the floor against my right hon. leader and his followers in this critical time of war. Such an innuendo ill becomes the hon. member for Frontenac, and I am proud to believe that such are not the sentiments of the people of Frontenac, but simply his personal feelings-and he is a very caustic critic. If the criticism had been a fair one, I would hardly have taken up the time of the House in replying to it.
I wish to make another reference to what the hon. gentleman said. On page 1270 of Hansard, he made use of this language:
I venture to say that men of the stamp of Howe, Tupper and Tilley would not approve the attitude of the Carvells and the Kytes. I venture to say that men of the stamp of Blake and Macdonald and Mackenzie would not endorse the attitude of men like the Tur-riffs. And, Mr. Speaker, men like Cartier would not endorse the attitude which the right hon. leader of the Opposition has taken since the war began.
1 ask you, Sir, if it is a fair criticism towards my hon. friend from Assiniboia

(Mr. Turriff) who has sent his son to the trenches in France where his blood now mingles with the soil, for such an innuendo to come across the floor of this House when we are in this dreadful struggle and the Liberals as well as the Tories are doing their full part in the interest of home and liberty? In these dreadful days, criticism is ill becoming on either side of the House, and I am glad to repeat that I do not believe that such are the sentiments of the people of Frontenac, but I believe it is matter of undue partisan criticism with the idea that some party capital may be made out of it.
