I am really sorry that so much levity should be displayed, because I think this is a solemn pcoasion. I am sorry that hon. gentlemen opposite seem to enjoy the kind of criticism that is made by the hon. member for Frontenac. To me it is a very serious thing that when reference is made to a criticism of the hon. member for Frpntenac imputing disloyalty to the Liberal party, hon. gentlemen opposite should lightly laugh.
There are just one or two other matters I wish to deal with. To my mind there are commodities just as important to the consumers of this country as wheat, which the Finance Minister recently put on the free list, and I want to give notice now that at the proper time-I cannot make the motion now as there is an amendment -already before the House-I shall move that:
Potatoes, and potatoes dried, desiccated, or otherwise prepared, be put on the free list.
In conclusion, the war situation to my mind is -such that we should endeavour to implement the promise of the Government, and if that cannot be done in
9 p.m. the ordinary way, other -means .of doing it should be found. But the Government of the day are responsible. I should like to see all parties, if

not the representatives of all views in this country, united in a common effort to implement the promise of the Government. The affairs of Canada, however are in the hands of the 'Government. They -are all powerful; they -are responsible to the people and to Empire, and it is up to them tp make the overtures.
It is up to them to make the -move; it is up to them to implement their promise. Even in fulfilling that promise we are not doing any more than our duty, and as a people we should not shirk any part of our duty in this crisis. We are fighting in a noble cause; we are fighting for liberty and right against oppression and wrong. It is the prayer of every one of us that the good cause may prevail. That prayer we should put into practice. With our "silver bullets," with our bodily strength, in every way, we should aid the Empire in this noble struggle for liberty and right.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. -Speaker (the Deputy Speaker, Mr. Rainville, in the -chair), I followed very closely the several addresses on the Budget delivered by the Minister of Finance, his colleague of the Cabinet and the hon. members on both sides of the House.
The hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Loggie) discussed the tariff at sufficient length to allow me to leave that question aside and devote my -attention to other fiscal matters.
The Minister of Finance -claimed a large share of credit because on the 31st of-March 1917, the trade of the country had reached the two billion mark. If you take into account the very great increase in the price of every article since 1911, and especially during 1917, it can be stated that our trade, both our imports and exports, has made no progress -since 1911-12. During the year 191112 our business totalled near to one billion dollars. Consult the statistics of every market and you will find that not only have prices doubled, but have increased in some instances three and four-fold. Take the wollen goods from England as an example: they used to sell at $1.75 to $1.90 a yard; to-day they -cost $4.25, $4.50 and up to $5.50. If the claim of increased trade of the hon. member were substantiated, our imports and exports should -amount, not to two billions, but to over three billions of dollars.
In 19.11-12, Mr. Speaker, we were exporting nothing for war purposes; this last year, although the Minister of Finance did not give us separately the figures relating to

the munitions exported, it is well known that there have been exported from Canada during 1916-17 munitions to the amount of at least two hundred millions of dollars.
I view with alarm, Mr. Speaker, the tremendous increase in the public debt. We are told by the Minister of Finance that at the end of the last fiscal year our debt exceeded $900,000,000, and that we could expect to see it reach by March 31, 1918, $1,500,000,000, on which nearly $75,000,000 will have to be paid for interest alone; add to that the soldiers' pensions estimated at $20,000,000 to $25,000,000, and you have a total of over $100,000,000 quite apart from the amount required for the ordinary expenditure, which cannot be less than $75,000,000. All that we shall have to pay not less than $150,000,000 to $175,000,000, which somewhat exceeds the ordinary and extraordinary revenue before and after the war.
When we are confronted by such alarming conditions, is it not time to take notice? All members of this House, whatever their politics, have at heart the welfare of the citizens of this Dominion. Again I say, Mr. Speaker, that in order to secure this welfare we must stop to reflect and see whither the present Administration is leading the affairs of the country.
Since the advent of the present Government in 1911, secured by methods most reprehensible, hon. gentlemen on the other side have constantly contrived to stir racial antagonism, not only in the province of Quebec, but especially in the province of Ontario and in one other province in the West, by representing the people of the province of Quebec as disloyal to the Crown and opposed to Great Britain as a whole. In this regard it may be contended that the poor welcome given at Montreal last Monday to the Postmaster General is proof of our disloyalty. I wish to say, however, that the Postmaster General only got what is coming to him in Montreal, and deserves to be dealt with similarly in every locality where, after preaching nationalism in 1910-11, he returns to advocate Imperialism.
I claim without fear of any contradiction that His Majesty -George V has no more loyal and devoted subjects than the French Canadians of the province of Quebec. It is recorded in our annals that but for the French Canadians, Canada would have been lost to England long ago. It is well Imown that at the time of the declaration of America's independence, in 1774, had the French Canadians consented to side with
the thirteen revolted colonies, the Stars and Stripes and not the Union Jack would float to-day over our Parliament buildings. The position taken at the time by the French Canadians, not known to all and purposely ignored by others, was prompted in the main by the Ro-man Catholic clergy of the province of Quebec, who called upon the French Canadian people to give -their lives, aye, the very last drop of their blood for the maintenance of that British dominion which was the bulwark of our rights and liberties in the province of Quebec, then the whole of Canada.
Later, in 1812, our friends from the other side of the line again invaded our territory. Who prevented the Americans conquest if not, to a large extent, the French Canadians of the province of Quebec?
It seems to me a marvel why our countrymen of Ontario, and in some western provinces, chiefly Manitoba, are so -much opposed to my race. No other race in Canada is subjected to such obloquy and abuse; even the Germans, the fiercest foe of Great Britain in the present war, would receive better treatment. This country is peopled by many different races, there are Russians, Italians, Jews, Austrians, Syrians, and Germans; they all seem to be accorded due respect by the English-speaking element of Ontario; it is even proposed to replace French by Russian in the schools of that province. The population of Quebec is represented as made u-p of ignorant slaves, without energy, incapable and unworthy of constituting a desirable nation. We are despised, Mr. Speaker; -we are even pilloried and yet, notwithstanding those insults, we remain loyal subjects of His Majesty when the bugle calls, summoning to the colours the descendants of those disloyal subjects, our youth leave home and friends, close their ranks around their country's flag, ready to defend it with their last -breath and the last drop of their blood. How many of those noble sons have I not seen myself, leaving fine positions, promising careers, their parents and their friends to run to the defence of the Allies and especially England? Even I myself had two sons who were my pride and my hope; they crossed overseas to fight for the liberty of the world and to secure to the small nations a place under the sun and some measure of freedom. One of my sons is already at the front and the other is in England training until the day when he shall join his brother. Thousands upon thousands of our sons have

responded to the call, and yet must we be told by a portion of the press in Ontario that we have done nothing. If the French Canadians have not enlisted, as the people of Ontario would have you believe, how is it that thousands of them have fallen on Europe's 'battlefields and that there are more of them ready to capture difficult positions that others cannot take. Let us not be deceived. It is an established fact that if the Germans have not taken Calais, all honour is due to the glorious 22nd battalion. At the battles of St. Julien, Festubert, Ypres, Langemarck, Courcelette and Vimy, our sons have given freely of their blood; and those battles are proofs to the whole world that the youth of the province of Quebec have remained worthy of their forebears, the discoverers, settlers, and defenders of this large and magnificent country of ours. More of them are wanted, Mr. Speaker; and still more of these brave scions of the French settlers in Canada.
Before doing more in that direction, should we not rouse .to consider whether really we have not gone far enough and whether our more sacred duty is not to strive to the utmost to secure the results asked of our efforts, that is to put under cultivation as large an area as possible and work to intensify production? How is it possible to reach that end? We first must seed the land and that requires, not only stocks of seed, but hands to put it in. How can we procure the necessary seed when the railways do not supply us with cars? Are you aware, Mr. Speaker, that the conditions are worse than they are thought to 'be? Last year there was a complete failure of the crops in the province of Quebec and in other provinces to some extent. The Quebec farmer must buy almost all his seed for this spring. At the present time it is impossible to get the potatoes or grain that we need. Notwithstanding the exorbitant prices, the farmers are willing to buy, provided the railway companies and the Department of Railways at Ottawa produce the necessary cars. Should not the Government take the same steps regarding those different products of the farm as they have done on behalf of the newspapers when they fixed the maximum price of newsprint? My idea is that it is the Government's duty to settle a maximum price for potatoes, oats, barley and wheat, whatever at least is needed as seed for this spring.
The plea is put forward that there are no available cars; but it is well known to those

who travel on the different railways in .Canada that the sidings are filled with empty cars; you, Mr. Speaker, who live in the town of St. Lambert, know that such is the case in the Grand Trunk yard in that locality. The same occurs at Point St. Charles and Turcot; also on the Canadian Pacific, at both Viger and Windsor stations, and on the Intercolonial, I believe, Mr. Speaker, that with very little exertion on his part, the Minister of Railways could furnish enough cars to allow the shipment of potatoes from New Brunswick to the farmers of my county, who need them for seeding purposes. It has been found impossible to proceed with seeding operations through lack of transportation facilities^ Judging from what is taking place and from the utterances of men who are fully aware of the requirements of the Allies, men like Lord Sliaughnessy, the Hon. Mr. Balfour, Lloyd George and our own Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) I must come to the conclusion that what is wanted most by the Allies is not more men and yet more men, but more food and still more food. That is what we are asked to furnish, but a large number of hands will be required to put in the crops, this spring, and to harvest them next fall. To secure farm help such salaries are asked that it will be impossible for the farmers to pay them. What is the remedy? I see only one possible suggestion: stop all recruiting for tne army; keep in Canada all those wno have enlisted; form battalions with available men who are willing to work on the land; give them a soldier's pay, and thus the farmers will secure the necessary help to sow the land and take in the crop, while paying a reasonable price; otherwise they cannot get the results expected of them.
The question of recruiting brings to mind the Postmaster General. No worse recruiting agent could be secured, because the people of Quebec put no faith in him whatever. Better try to recruit farm help than to enlist soldiers to help him to patch up the British flag which he claimed our ancestors had been forced to bore full of holes in order to breathe the air of liberty. If the Postmaster General's patriotism goes to the length he would fain have us believe, why not give up his salary to help recruiting farm hands for the province of Quebec?
We were told by the Minister of Finance on behalf of the Government that the fiscal year ending on March 31 last brought a
MA\ 10, 1917
surplus of $60,000,000. That money, Mr. Speaker, has 'been taken from the people in the form of duties and taxes. Speaking personally, I should have preferred to see that money applied to prepare the aftermath of the war, keeping the war expenses by themselves to be reclaimed from Germany in the treaty of peace.
During the whole of forty-one years, Mr. Speaker, I, as a merchant, sold articles of all kinds. I am sorry to say that during the later years most of what I sold was imported from Geftnany. Why not see to it that industries having to do with the manufacture of similar articles be established in this country? We are particularly well situated for the purpose, because Canada has a boundless supply of raw material.
Yesterday I listened to the hon. member for Eouville (Mr. Lemieux) on technical education. If, instead of applying to war purposes our surplus of sixty millions, a portion of it had been used to promote technical education in Canada, such a policy in my estimation would have been the part of wisdom and in the interest of the Canadian people.-
The Government has appointed a commission to inquire into the country's needs after the war and suggest the best methods to adopt. The return has been brought down but I fail to see what measures the Government is taking on the lines suggested. The country's development calls for urgent and immediate action; let the Government be' up and doing, or else at the next election the people will put into their places men capable of fostering the interests of the nation. During the recess, I had occasion to visit a portion of the province of Quebec which had been criticised by hon. gentlemen opposite when the right hon. leader of the Opposition thought fit to build the Transcontinental. I visited, Mr. Speaker, the Abitibi region, which had been represented as being altogether unproductive and inhabitable; it was claimed to 'be a waste of money to build a railway from Cochrane to Quebec. I was anxious to see for myself. Let me state that in insisting on the Transcontinental being built from Cochrane to Quebec the right hon. leader of the Opposition showed great foresight. When the resources of Canada's granary, the great western prairies, shall have been exhausted, we shall find in the North of the province of Quebec, in the Abitibi fields, another granary that will furnish, not only to the province of Quebec, but to the whole
world, the wheat required for the sustenance of the peoples of the earth.
There is a defect, however, in the Trans- >
continental line from Cochrane to Quebec. The service is a poor one. For the last couple of years there has been some improvement, but the service is still unsatisj factory. There are two trains per day three times a week. Why not have only one train a day every day in the week? The men on the road are exceedingly careless. Freight cars are allowed to stay whole weeks at stations next to the points they are billed for,' and if the owners protest, they are laughed at, if not given worse treatment. A little good will in the Department of Railways, and some fairness towards the province of Quebec, would soon secure to that favoured region thrifty settlers living happy and contented on fertile lands and in an ideal climate. Although I made the trip during the winter, I could see that the railway had been fairly well constructed, except for some slopes and curves between the Fitzpatrick and O'Brien sections, which have doubtless been changed with the object of injuring the road. Elsewhere the road is perfect. I hope the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) will take my remarks in good part and do his utmost to right those conditions.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think I have stated in all frankness and without prejudice, the situation as I view it and as many citizens view it also. And the situation being such, is it wise to continue recruiting for the war, when there is no necessity of more soldiers, unless it be to permit some people to cross to Europe for the purpose of patching the British flag bored full of holes, that French Canadians may breathe the air of liberty, as was stated in 1911, by my hon. friend, Mr! Blondin, at a meeting at St. Hyacinthe, where I had the pleasure of replying to him. In my opinion, it would be too costly to send over certain persons who are not wanted on the one hand and who would Be of no use if they went.
I wish to add also that, in view of the urgent needs of the country, the Government should take the necessary steps to repatriate as soon as possible all soldiers who have been declared unfit for the service and who are paid $1.10 per day and fed in the military camps in England, where they are of no practical value to Great Britain or Canada. There are nearly one thousand of those in England. There are others whose names should be taken off the pay-list, col-

onels, lieutenant-colonels, captains, majors, lieutenants, who are merely good to show off in military parades and walk the streets of London. Even here in Canada we have quite a number of those officers whom we pay out of the public money drawn from the people's tax money, who are of no service whatever in the trenches and have lived in sloth long enough at the public expense.
We are being preached to practice economy, Mr. Speaker; I agree with the preaching, but I disagree with the preachers, who lack faith in their own teachings. They practice the very opposite of what they advocate. The returns from the various departments of the inside and outside service furnish ample proof of that fact. There has been a scandalous number of extraordinary appointments since 1911. On a visit to the Montreal post-office last winter, partly through curiosity and partly on business, I was astounded to see the large number of clerks in the various offices who had nothing else to do but order one another about doing nothing.
We have had also, Mr. Speaker, a return showing the number of Liberal employees discharged under the present Administration and the number appointed in their places. Can it fie believed that, according to the return, ten thousand Liberals were discharged and twenty-one thousand friends of the Government appointed in their stead. Appointments have been made without any respect for the Civil Service Act, in fact in direct violation of the Act. Positions have been given to persons who can barely read, even on the staff of the Library, where surely of all places educated men are required. That employee was given a fat salary of $1,200, his appointment was made to date back six months before he entered on his work and he was granted an indemnity for lodging for six months prior to his taking up his duties because the Parliament buildings were burned down. We have here, Mr. Speaker, a sample of the manner in which the affairs of the country are administered by ministers who go into the cities and throughout the country clamouring for the strictest economy by the people. I was right in stating that those preachers lack faith in their own teachings.
A word as to National Service. If the desire was to obtain the information which we are told was aimed at, that is to find out how many people were disposed to work in the munition factories or on the land, the

only way was to put the questions frankly, honestly and without any reticence. The cards had two queries which left a great deal to conjecture; they are questions 23 and 24. Many electors asked me if they should sign the National Service card. "Do so," I said, " but beware how you reply to the last two questions. If you are willing to go anywhere and in any capacity, answer 'yes'; if not, say 'no.' If you are ready to work in Canada in the munition factories or on the farms, say 'yes'; otherwise, write 'no.' " It may be that only a few cards have been returned from the county I have the honour to represent; the people are not to blame, because it is a constituency made up chiefly of farmers. A farmer with 125 or 150 acres in cultivation and often with only one son to help cannot be expected to leave his own work and go on some other farm, especially in view of the fact that we are requested to intensify production. *
Before 1911, the Government led by the present right hon. leader of the Opposition ' (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) spent $98,000,000 for the administration of the country. We were taken to task then for our extravagance, our wasteful methods. What shall be said of a Government who spend for the same work the enormous sum of $172,000,000 in round numbers? Is it to be wondered that the people are complaining under the burden of taxes and repent of their sin of 1911? I do feel, Mr. Speaker, that when, at the bugle call, the officers will review the ranks, calling upon the electors to rally around the colours-not those of war but the Liberal standard-there will be among the hon. gentlemen opposite many bitter tears and gnashing of the teeth. We on your left, Mr. Speaker, have cause for congratulation when we see the very principles advocated and defended by the liberals in 1911 and condemned, censured and vilified by those who attained power by means of those tactics, recognized to-day by their erstwhile opponents as sound; for now that they are in power, the Conservatives adopt and apply those very Liberal principles, in connection with such questions, as the navy and reciprocity.
Doubtless you remember, Mr. Speaker, how the electoral campaign was conducted in Quebec in 1911. You recall the terrible scarecrow that was made of the Laurier navy, the terror that was struck into women and children by the description of the horrors of war and how mothers were terrified because their sons would be snatched from

their arms and sent to be butchered on the seas of China and Japan. More than any, I know the terrors which were spread during the campaign of 1911 in the Province of Quebec by Nationalists; my opponent in the election was one of the strongest adherents of Nationalism. Previously I had the opportunity especially in Drummond-Arth-baska, of meeting some of those self-styled Nationalists, as the Hon. Mr. Nantel, exMinister of Inland Bevenue, who accepted a commissionership on the Eailway Commission, knowing full well the chastisement which the electors of Terrebonne had in store for him when he should seek re-election. Those who had such a dread of the tin-pot navy, -as it was called in 1911, are quite satisfied now to have those vessels protecting the Atlantic and Pacific seaboards against possible invasion. To such an extent did they go in their acceptance of the Liberal policies, that at the opening of hostilities they bought two submarines that had -been built for the Chilean Government but refused as being defective. Our Government bought them in spite of all, hoping to use them in the defence of -the Pacific coast, but unfortunately the two boats behaved in Canadian waters as they behaved before the Chilean experts; when they -attempt to submerge they plunged to the bottom and it will be necessary to use torpedoes in order to raise them. If we are in a position to-day to build ships in Canada for the Allies of Great Britain, it is due to the policy inaugurated in 1910 by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). As a matter of fact, if the Canadian Vickers established their shipyards in Montreal, it is because Sir Wilfrid Laurier had decided in 1910 upon a programme of naval construction, the ships to be built in Canada, by Canadian labour, for the benefit of Canada instead of handing over, as was this Government's policy in 1903, $35,000,000 for the -construction of three dreadnoughts for Great Britain, who did not require them.
I could take hours to dilate on the bad administration which the Canadian electorate accidentally voted to power in 1911, but not to-day. The people are only waiting for a chance to correct that mistake. I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that the time is not far off when the opportunity will be given the people to make amends by placing at the helm of the state men who have -the people's interest at heart, men able to govern without stirring racial and religious animosities between the different nationalities that constitute the Canadian people. To that end, Mr. Speaker, there is only one thing to do: it is to recall to power that great Canadian, that greatest of Canadians, the Eight Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who for fifteen years has led the country through an era of prosperity.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take up a little of the time of the House to discuss that part of the Budget speech which has reference to the taxation of industrial profits. When the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) delivered his Budget speech last year and singled out the manufacturers as fit subjects for taxation, it appeared to me then as an unjust and unwise procedure. When this measure was before the committee, I think the minister assured the House that it would be in force for three years and would not be disturbed. I have not consulted Hansard, but I think if you will look up the record you will find that when this measure was going through the committee the minister so expressed himself, stating that this taxation of 25 per cent upon profits over and above 7 per cent on corporations and 10 per cent on partnerships, would not be disturbed for three years. But, unfortunately, the minister has changed his mind. If it was an unjust tax in the first instance, I am very sure that it has not been modified any by this new departure of coming back again and imposing a further tax of 50 per cent on all profits between 15 and 20 per cent and 75 per cent on all profits over 20 per cent. Industrial companies of all kinds are subject to fat and lean years, periods of prosperity and periods of great depression when

it is a hard problem for them to keep afloat, meet their obligations and pay dividends. Many of them pass their dividends. We are told in sacred history of a king of Egypt who, at one time, had a dream that troubled him. He consulted all the wise men of the realm, and finally he found one who could interpret the meaning of his dream. The interpretation was to the effect that they were then to have a number of years of great prosperity and abundance, to. be followed by another period of years of great leanness,	no	prosperity, no	crop,nothing. The king, in his wisdom, provided	out	of the	rich	years
a fund to carry his people and his country through the period of lean years. It would have been wise if the Minister of Finance had looked up a little sacred history and if he had done so perhaps he would have thought it wise not to put the whole burden on the manufacturers, 'because we are going through a period of some prosperity. It cannot be denied, and I am not here to deny, that the manufacturers in most lines are prosperous. But, it is also true that the managers of nearly every industrial concern, if they make any money, instead of paying great big dividends and pocketing the money, generally invest it in extensions and additions to the plant, thereby increasing production and building up the country. This measure of taxation placing the whole of the burden of providing revenue to meet the war expenditures on the manufacturers alone is striking a blow at industry. It is striking a blow at the men of energy and ability who are willing to put their best efforts and their money into industrial enterprises. The minister said that he had collected from this source last year some 512,000,000, and he expected to collect, I think, 525,000,000 or more next year. He thought that everybody was perfectly happy because he had not received a single protest. Because people do not protest, because they do not kick up a row, because they are willing to bear a certain amount of the burden, is that a reason for soaking them a little more? I for one am not here to protest, find any fault or make any objection, as a manufacturer, to paying my fair share of the burdens of this war, providing the burden is laid upon all, rich and poor. The poor will pay according to their means and the rich will do the same. Take, for instance, the case of two men, the sons of a rich father. The father divides up and gives each of them a large fortune. One of the sons chooses to go into industrial busi-83
ness, into manufacturing, and he puts every dollar of his money and all the energy he has into the enterprise, and possibly injures his health by overwork. The other son takes hisi money and invests it in good securities. He sits back in his easy chair, blips his coupons when they come due; he	is	found	in	the Southin the winter	and in	the	North inthe summer at a fashionable watering place or	a	place	of	recreation.What I ask is, is	this	man a specialfavourite who should be treated with special consideration? He does not do anything, he does not employ anybody, he is simply living on the energies of his father before him. He has put the money 'he inherited into investments, and has in this way made some money. But the other man has put his money in industry; he employs a large number of people, he pays good wages, perhaps ruins his health in doing so, and builds up a business and made interest on his money, but he is made the goat because he cannot get away. The minister has said:	I't is true we might
resort to income tax and many other sources of taxation, but it would require a lot of machinery and work, .and it is hard to get at them. Again I ask, suppose that two men are walking down the street, one a manufacturer and the other a professional man, or some other man, and they commit a crime that is punishable by penitentiary. Warrants are got out and the authorities seek for the offenders. They find the manufacturer-he cannot get away, he is tied down to his business. The other man skips to Mexico or some other place. They know where he is, but it is going to he a trouble to get him. What would you propose doing with the man whom you have? Would you hang him and make him suffer the penalty of the two because the other man is a little hard to get? There is just as much logic in that as there is in the minister saying that because it is a little hard to reach the man who spends his time clipping his bond coupons and looking after his income, because it takes more machinery to reach him we will*leave him alone; but the man we have got we will hang or crucify, or do anything else to him we like, and make him bear the whole burden. A striking case came under my notice a couple of years ago. A man in the pulpwood business had got out a large stock of pulpwood, he got his drive in, and started up his dressing or rossing mill. The first week he was operating the mill it took fire and was



burned down. He had a big lot of wood on hand, but no mill to dress it. He went to his bank to borrow the necessary capital to rebuild. The bank said: In the first place, would we have furnished you money to make your drive and you have exhausted your line of credit? In the second place, it is not customary for the banks to loan money on long terms. You want money to 'build a plant; we cannot lend it to you. He looked around and came across some of these gentlemen whom I have described, who had some money. He told them his story. He said: I have my limit, a large tract of freehold lands; I am willing to give you a first mortgage on it; I want to raise $50,000 to build my mill; my limit is worth at least five times the money I want to borrow. They said: Very well, we will loan you $50,000 and take a first mortgage on your property, but we will take the first mortgage for $62,500, and we will charge you eight per cent interest on $62,500. There was no other remedy, he had to build his mill, he could not help himself. He borrowed the money, he gave a mortgage for $62,500 and received $50,000 in cash. These gentlemen are not touched by this legislation, they are not affected. I want to know from this House if that appeals to the members as anything like honest or sound logic, or sound taxation. I for one do not think it is. I am not opposed to paying 25 per cent, or 50 per cent, or 75 per cent, or the whole profits if necessary, provided that everybody else is treated in the same way, but I see no reason why I should be singled out. It is said by some: Oh, the manufacturer is making big money and he can afford to pay this taxation. Yes, we are making some money but what about the farmer? What about the price of wheat, $3 a bushel while the normal price [DOT] is about 90 cents? What about 'the price of pork and cattle and other lines of agricultural produce? I was talking to a man in Montreal last week on this very question, and this gentleman told me that there were two firms of lawyers in Montreal, each man representing his own individual firm, and the income of each of these men was considerably over $100,000 this year from the office alone. I admit that they were probably the leading lawyers of the city, but this was their income from their office alone, to say nothing of their investments-and I am sure they would have investments because men of that income generally have some- I want to know from this House if there is any reason why men of this class, why 
men of all classes, should not contribute their fair 'share to the taxes that are necessary. We have got to be taxed, we are at war and it is every man's business to contribute his share and to do it cheerfully; but it is not right, it is not just, it is not honest, on the part of the Government to put the whole burden on the manufacturer alone. The minister does not seem to be quite satisfied, it is his second dose to one particular branch of manufacture. A short time ago the minister thought it wise on his part to fix the rate of newsprint at two and one-half cents, which is at least a cent a pbund less than it can be produced for.

speechtext:
The minister, I assume,
would deny this, but the way he figures the cost of paper is the cost, taking it from the tree until it is delivered in a sheet of paper. The way I figure the cost of news print is as follows:	The selling value of
sulphite pulp is not less than $100, say an average of $100, and it requires. 500 pounds of sulphite pulp for the manufacture of a ton of news print. In addition to that about 1,600 pounds of ground wood pulp is required for a ton of paper. That is 2,100 pounds, as there is about 5 per cent of waste in the conversion of pulp into paper. That pulp is worth to-day at least, selling retail as fast as we can make it, $40 to $50 a ton, put it at the lowest figure, $40; and 1,600 pounds of ground wood pulp at $40 is $32. You have $25 worth of sulphite pulp and $32 worth of ground wood pulp before you go to your conversion at all. Add to that your coal, labour, size and resin and the other necessities, and it will bring your pulp up to at least $70 a ton before you get a cent of profit out of it. I maintain that the cost of your paper is the value of the pulp that you can quickly sell for cash and not have to wait for your money or ship it, simply load it and get youT money. That is the condition of the paper business at this present moment, and the minister, in his wisdom-no, I think not in his wisdom, I think he listened to the stories and the arguments of the publishers and did not wait to hear what the manufacturers had to say before he made up his mind and passed judgment on the question-fixed the price at 2J cents. If he had been patient and had waited until he heard the arguments on both sides, he would have seen the wisdom of being a little fairer in the matter than he has been.

the right hon. leader of the Opposition, if I remember rightly, asked the minister the other day if an Order in Council had been passed fixing the price of newsprint paper, to which, I understand, he replied that no such order had been passed; that the parties had come to an understanding among themselves. Let me tell you how they came to an understanding. I was not at the meeting, but I was told about it by our manager, who was there. The minister simply told those present: if you do not accept 2J cents, I will make it 2J; so you had better accept what has been proposed. That is how they consented to it-with a club over their heads. They had to accept it. Perhaps the minister understands all about the conditions respecting the pulp and paper business, and perhaps he does not. I want to tell this House something about it. Prior to the month of March, 1916, some of the biggest paper industries on this continent had to re-organize; they were unable to pay even the interest on their preferred stock. In March, 1916, approximately 100,000 tons of ground wood pulp were piled in Canada, and there was, besides, a large amount on the other side. Trade had not been very good, the mills were running only four or five days a week; there was an over-production of ground wood pulp. The increased demand and the increased price commenced about March, 1916, and although the water condition last year was a good one and water was plentiful, that whole surplus of ground wood pulp has disappeared, together with whatever additional wood that could be ground. There is at present very little surplus ground wood pulp. Sulphite pulp and chemical pulp of all kinds is manufactured by a chemical process requiring but little power, and if there is a shortage of it the manufacturer can force his production and thus meet the difficulty. But ground wood pulp, 75 or 80 per cent of which goes into newsprint, is manufactured by a mechanical process and cannot be economically or successfully made by any other power than water-power. For instance, it requires 70 to 75 horse power working 24 hours to grind one ton of pulp, and if you generate power by steam or coal to grind pulp it will cost you so much that you cannot make newsprint of it. It has to be made by cheap power, and if the Almighty doe3 not give you water you cannot grind pulp. This surplus that was piled out last March, together with the additional output, having been exhausted, what will happen 834
if we have a dry season this year? I doubt very much whether the newsprint people will get all the paper they want, no matter what legislation the Finance Minister may adopt to help them out, because legislation cannot produce water, and nobody can make pulp without water. Although the price of nearly every commodity has gone up very materially, the manufacturers, of their own free-will, before any demand was made upon them by the Government, offered to supply the Canadian publishers with paper at 3 cents, which certainly would give them no profit. Under present conditions I do not know what induced the minister to take the course that he did; I know that in other lines of business the profits are very much higher than in the newsprint paper business. These he has not seen fit to touch, and wisely so; I am sorry that he was not as wise in Teepect to the newsprint business'. Anyway, the general effect will 'be that capital will hesitate to put money into anything connected with the paper business, or into any other business in respect of which the Government sees fit to fix prices, especially unreasonably low. I was talking to a man in Montreal last week, a man of big means, who has the ear of many of the financial people of this country. He told me that he bad made all necessary arrangements for the construction of a very large pulp and paper mill, but he said that when he went to New York and told his people that the Government had practically fixed the price of newsprint and was taking a big part of the profits he could not get them to listen to him for a minute. I believe that this Government is sincere and wants to build up the country, but I want to tell hon. gentlemen that interfering with the prices of commodities and putting the burden of taxation on a few people is not the way to build up the country. I candidly believe that the minister's apparent willingness to place all the burdens on the manufacturer alone and to let everybody else go scot-free has not been heard the last of. I notice that this measure of taxation, strange to say, is fairly popular, and one reason for its popularity is that it will touch only about 5 per cent of the population. If the minister has the courage of his convictions -and I believe that he has-he will frame up some tariff or some legislation whereby everybody in Canada will bear his fair share of the burden. If he does that he will not hear a whimper from anybody; every one will cheerfully bear his share of the burden and do his share. Let us con-

sider what has occurred in the case of the American people since the war started. At the beginning of the war they were under just as much obligation as England was to protect Belgium, tout they did not fulfil their Obligations under the Treaty. That was the first thing that made them feel rather ashamed when they began to realize that they had held back and allowed Belgium to toe ruined by Germany. After the sinking of the Lusitania occurred, if you met Americans and spoke to them, you would find that they had rather a feeling of shame and that they would make excuses for the notes that were written toy their President. But since the Americans have come out and said: We will do our share from now on, eveTy American is smiling; he feels happy; he feels that he is no longer living securely at his ease behind other people's energies and efforts. The same thing applies to the taxation that is necessary for the carrying on of this war. If the Government had the courage they should have and fixed the burdens that should toe borne by every one equally, every one w.ould be happy and contented. But under present conditions there is not very much happiness amongst the manufacturers, whether of paper or of anything else. I suppose people will say: " Well, McCrea is speaking because this touches him." McCrea is no slacker. I will stand up and do my share, but I do npt want to do some one else's share. I want every man, woman and child who have the ability to do it, to pay their fair share, and I think they will be perfectly satisfied to do so.	[DOT]	.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Minister of Labour this afternoon, delivered a speech in, which he eulogized himself and the Department of Labour in every way that he possibly could. With that I have no fault to find. He is satisfied with himself, -and perhaps the rest of us ought to be satisfied with him; perhaps the country ought to toe satisfied with

him, but strange to say, even although he will admit himself that he has made a moet excellent Minister of Labour, the country will be loath to agree with him. There were some things that he particularly laboured upon, namely, the price of various commodities, such as coal, foodstuffs, etc., and yet when I questioned him, it appeared to me that the Minister of Labour sidestepped in answering those particular questions which are pertinent-although he did not seem to think so-to the carrying on of the war and to the welfare of the people of Canada. He sidestepped as only the Minister of Labour can; for the pure and simple reason, in my opinion, that he had no other course to pursue, because he had done nothing in regard to the matter. In his address this afternoon, his- defence of the Department of Labour was that he had sent out many questions to many dealers; that the questions had been answered; that the dealers had told him that they had so much produce on hand; that it had cost them so much money and that they could sell it for so much money in order to make a profit. The minister, however, did not tell us that they sold it at a reasonable profit.
The minister sent out ' questionnaires ' as he called them; I am not familiar with the word, but I suppose it answers the purpose. These cards were sent out, and the answers came in. The minister found out what a particular thing cost and what it was being sold for, and then, to use his own words, he * got after them.' The Minister of Labour may have got answers, but by this Order in Council he shifted the responsibility on to the shoulders of the township councils. From the time the Liberal party went out of power in 1911 down to the present day of grace there has been no government in this or in any other country that has appointed the same number of commissions in order to avoid responsibility, as has this Government. The Minister of Labour has followed this thing out in a way that he thinks is commendable to himself and to the Tory party, but the people do not think so. What did the Minister of Labour say this afternoon? He said they had looked up the cost of foodstuffs all down the line, and in every case they had taken care of the matter. But, Mr. Speaker, the proof of the pudding is in the eating. Never has the Conservative party lacked leadership so much as at the present moment, when we are'at the greatest crisis in our history.

speechtext:
My hon. friends may
laugh, but let them tell us what they have done. They may laugh in their complacency, but the question the people of this country are asking is the very question I am asking to-night. The hon. Minister of Labour entered into a long dissertation this afternoon as to what this Government had done in the interests of labour and the common people of this country, and my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) said truly that the minister was only reiterating and reiterating what he had been telling the House ever since the session opened in twenty-one columns of Hansard. But, as I said before, the proof of the pudding is in the eating. The minister tells us he has sent out his men, that they have looked into these things, and that he has read such cards as he has picked up here and there in his department, But does the fact that the dealers have filled in the cards showing the amount of stuff they have on hand, prove that they are selling their goods to the people of this country at only a fair profit? The minister mentioned Hamilton. He pointed to that city as if everything there was as it ought to be. Let me read to the House from a report of the last meeting of the Hamilton City Council:-
Some startling information regarding the holding of food and fuel supplies in this city was given to-night to the City Council by Alderman Langes, chairman of the High Cost of Living Committee. Alderman Langes presented a report of the Committee's activity that showed some men were holding potatoes in large quantities here, and trow indifferent the Government appears to be regarding the situation. Following this statement, he submitted a resolution that the facts be submitted to the Government, and that it be asked to prosecute these dealers under the Order in Council passed last fall. This was carried unanimously.
Might I say, in passing, that although the Minister of Labour said that his policy was to get after the dealers as soon as he found they were charging exorbitant rates, up to this very day the Government, although they have the power, have not entered one single prosecution against dealers who have been charging exorbitant rates; not one. The report goes on:-
Alderman Langes said that they had learned that one Arm alone in this city was holding between 4,000 and 5,000 bags of potatoes, which it had bought at from $1.03 to $2.00 per bag. They also had information that some coal dealers were holding large quantities of coal from last winter that could he sold at slightly above $S per ton and for which they asked as high as $12 during the coal shortage. Bakers were also acting contrary to the Combines Act.

The Minister of Labour would not allow me to go on with my questions in the House this afternoon as to whether this report was true or not. He appealed to you, Sir, and I was ruled out of order. Let hon. gentlemen listen to what follows:-
This information was placed before W. T. O'Connor, K.C., representing the Labour Department. Mr. O'Connor complimented the Committee (Hamilton Committee) on its activities, and stated that no other city in Canada had gone so far under authority of the Order in Council. He left for Ottawa, promising that some one from the department would be here in two or three days. The Committee waited two weeks, but no one came. Word was sent to Ottawa and J. C. Imlay came to the city from the Department at Ottawa. He promised that necessary action would be taken but no word has since been heard from the Department. Alderman Langes said that he believed that both , Mr. O'Connor and Mr. Imlay were sincere, and he did not like to blame the Government but felt they should demand an explanation. He then presented the resolution referred to. "We have gone as far as we can," he added, "and the Government must either take action now or refuse."
Has anybody heard a noise like the Government taking action? I have not heard it; the people have not heard it; Hamilton has not heard it. As is usual with the Department of Labour, nothing is being done; the whole matter is in abeyance, but some day, no doubt-not now, because there is no precedent for it-the Minister of Labour will wake up and look into the matter. The report goes on:-
Mayor -Booker said no person in that Council could fall to regret that the Government had been s*o slow in taking action on food and on other conditions. It did not appear to have the backbone that was shown in the United States.

speechtext:
Wilson has plainly laid
down t!he policy, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) need not quibble. And Wilson has not been at war three years before laying down that policy.

It did not appear to have the backbone that was shown in the United States.
Strange, that the friends of the Government in Hamilton should compare them with the United States!
They were merely asking it to protect the people instead of catering to manipulators.
If the Solicitor General can get a grain of comfort from this report upon the action of the Government-and no doubt that report was made regardless of friend or foe politically-he is welcome to it. While what I have read shows the state of affairs existing in the city of Hamilton to-day, it is only a sample of what exists throughout the province of Ontario and throughout the whole Dominion. It only goes to show, more strongly than anything I might say, that it is high time this Government waked up and exercised some kind of control over the prices of fuel and of food and prevented the holding of excessive quantities by dealers. The Solicitor General smiles. I knew he would; he always smiles when he has nothing to say. But the fact remains, and the Solicitor General and the rest of the Government would do well to bear it in mind, that the common people are looking to the Government for relief from the present excessive prices. The Minister of Labour this afternoon, in his own easy way, and without knowing what was doing here or what was doing there-just trying to get over the hill with the least inconvenience-said: " The working people have more money than ever before; they are better	off than ever before."
They have more money, but they are not better off. They have more dollars, but a dollar does not purchase the same quantity of food and fuel that it purchased five years ago. Large wages are paid? Who said anything to the contrary? But the average worker is not as well off to-day as he was five years ago with a much smaller wage. The Government cannot get away from this fundamental truth, that what is needed to-day, as it never was needed before, is some direction as to foodstuffs and fuel; what is needed to-day is that the Government should afford that direction even if they have to name a food dictator as has been done in England, or even though they should take these products and regulate their distribution. And they should do that irrespective of whether the effect is to hurt or help their political friends. This is what is needed for the good of Canada, and nobody will admit it more quickly than the Minister of Trade and

Commerce (Sir George Foster) himself, for he realizes as no other member of the Government, or the Government as a whole, realizes, that what the country wants to-day is guidance on economic lines. You may say what you like, you [DOT] may use what sophistry you like, but the fact remains that, irrespective of the Minister of Labour's-I cannot call it a speech, but I will call it an attempted explanation-what the people are looking for is for the Government to give them some lead, in order that they may be relieved from their present necessities which are dire. The people of Canada are facing a crisis, and the sooner the Government realize that fact, the better it will he for the country. You cannot have a cataclysm such as that which has come upon the world to-day without having it affect every nation and every dependency of every nation that is engaged in war- and Canada is in it to the hilt. The sooner the people and the Government recognize that fact, and the sooner they realize that every step that is possible must be taken to conserve every resource we have, the greater will be the help that we can give "to the Empire, the more effective will be the sacrifice which we are making of our best blood and best fibre for the upholding of all that we believe to be just. I doubt that the people of Canada, wealthy, prospering as they are, realize that their present condition is a superficial prosperity and that the day of reckoning must come. But such is the fact, and the sooner we prepare for that day of reckoning the better for the Dominion and for the Empire. These are plain truths.
I have one word to say in conclusion. The hon. member for L'Islet (Mr. Paquet) spoke of the Bonne Entente. It would be far better for all elements in this Dominion if they would recognize and live up to a real bonne entente. This country is great, perhaps one of the greatest under God's sun. But if we are still to keep up in the years to come the schisms that certain elements have fostered in the years past, we cannot get the best results from the whole people.
There are elements, and every sane man knows it, that cannot be absolutely controlled in this country. But there are certain other elements which ought to be big and broad enough, and Canadian enough, to see that the fires of these certain other elements are not fanned into flame but that instead they ought to be met in a way that will promote the best Canadianism
because, by promoting the best Canadianism, you promote the best Imperialism. These flames ought not to be fanned or nurtured but every man who has the interests of the country at heart, ought to sink these miserable differences for the good of the whole, stand by Canadianism, and Canadianism only, and make this country what it ought to be and what my leader has attempted to make it-
