I was sure I would get a response from the other side; they could not help it. Let us try, I say, to make of Canada what my right hon. leader has attempted to make her: one united Canada, irrespective of any class or creed, in order that our country may become absolutely a nation within an Empire, and a prop and stay of the British Empire.
Mr. ARTHUR B. COPP (Westmorland): Mr. Speaker, during the progress of the debate it apparently has been in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House should not take up time in offering any criticism, making suggestions or discussing public matters generally. That is not new on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite, but more emphasis has been placed upon it during this debate than I have ever noticed before. If I had no other reason for saying a few words on this occasion I would have a good text in the pamphlet which I received through the mail this afternoon. I find this pamphlet endorsed:
Address delivered by Lt.-General Sir Sam Hughes, K.C.B., M.P., to his constituents of Victoria and Haliburton counties at Lindsay, Ont., April 28th. 1917.
I have not had an opportunity, Sir, ,of reading this speech through very carefully but I have scanned it hurriedly and some of the paragraphs in the address have appealed to me as a veTy good reason why not only hon. gentlemen on this side of the House but hon. gentlemen who were the confreres of the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence might consider carefully and sincerely what is their duty in regard to the public matters that are now occupying the attention of this House and the country. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that the members of the Opposition offering criticisms are, to a certain extent, wanting in loyalty and patriotism and they go so far as to suggest that while we are offering these criticisms we are adding fuel to the fire and

giving confidence and assistance to our enemies in" this great war.
This afternoon we were treated tp an exhibition rarely, if ever, witnessed in this or any other deliberative assembly, not by one of the ordinary members of this House but by a <minisiter of the Grown (Mr. Crothers) who took us to task for talking up so much of the time of the House unnecessarily and wasting not only the time of the House but of hon. members who -are 'Sent here as -the representatives of the -people. He was so careful that he figured out how much time was actually wasted in the discussion of public affairs by hon. gentlemen .on this side of the House. He figured out that we were wasting so many hours per day for so -many days. That hon. gentleman during the address he delivered in this House a few evenings ago, took up aJbout two hours of the time discussing the administration of the Labour Department, of which (he is in control. To-day -he saw fit to take two hours more discussing the very same question, as pointed out by my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) this -afternoon. Therefore, we have four hours of the time of the House taken up and to follow the mode of calculation of my hon. friend this afternoon, 200 members of this House were each kept here for four hours, which would mean 800 hours altogether, and as the House sits about six hours a day, the minister consumed 133 days of the time of the members discussing one question in this Parliament. In spite of the self-adoration of the minister, I doubt very much whether the information he gave to the members of this House and the people of the country is worth 133 days' time. But the hon. gentleman took that time, and while he took that time he complained that we should take any time whatever discussing these public questions. I would like to ask my hon. friend what the Opposition are here for if they are not to make any statements, offer any criticisms or make any suggestions, or to represent the minority of the pepple. I contend, Sir, that it is not only the right but the duty of hon. members of this side of the House to discuss public questions, because iit is only through criticism and discussion -by hon. gentlemen on -this side of the House that public matters get to the people through the public press giving reports which are taken from what takes place in this great theatre of public discussion. My hon. friend was very muoh alarmed because of the time that have taken up, -but I would point out that the 
hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) took up the time of the House the other evening criticising the Government of the day more severely than any member on this side of the House has done, -and that he made the statement that the Department of Labour had absolutely done nothing to help the people by reason of the policy which they had pursued in past years and particularly during the present Parliament. Buit to go further back than that, what do we learn from the hon. the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes)? In the speech he made to his constituents, earlier in his remarks, I find this statement:
Since then, however,-
That is since making his speech in the House in the early part of the session.
-several members and others have learned a few of the facts, and they regret that I did not inform them at the time, so that prompt and decisive action in the premises could have been taken by the party.
Now what does that mean? The exMinister of Militia -and Defence says that his own confreres told him that they were -sorry and regretted -that he had not made known to them circumstances that had been taking place and conditions that were -affecting the public welfare of this country while he was one of the members of the Cabinet ' doing the business of this country. Well, Sir, they have those facts now. I would ask my -hon. friends if the statement made by the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence can mean anything -but that there have been bickerings, dissatisfaction, pulling in opposite directions, among the members of the Government in regard to the business of carrying on the war, instead of their working harmoniously together in the interests of the people and the conduct of the war to a final triumphant conclusion. The ex-minister says that these bickerings occurred not only recently, but two or three years ago.
But let us go a little further. We find that the ex-Minister of Militia makes certain charges against his colleagues in the Government. Those charges have been read to the House on different occasions, and I do not propose to put many of the quotations on Hansard that I see before me in this pamphlet that has been received by me to-night. But there are'one ot two to which I wish to refer. He refers in one place to trouble in the Cabinet when he returned from Valcartier. A sub-committee of the Cabinet had been -appointed to look after some purchasing contracts, and he says:-

"When I had informed the proposed committee of their appointment and of my plans I suggested that they should immediately secure options on all commodities known to he wanted. Prices were then normal. At once options were secured on large numbers of horses on woollen goods, and on certain powder commodities. It was therefore rather a rude shock to my proposed committee to find that authority had been given to a sub-committee as stated ; but there was nothing to be done but frankly inform the parties from whom the options had been received of the change in plan and to cancel tne options.
What does that mean? It means as plainly as the English language can convey any meaning that the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence had made arrangements and secured options on the requirements of different supplies of horses and all of these things quietly, while prices were normal and before they commenced to soar on account of the war. He tells us in a statement to his constituents that this was all swept away, that the options that bad been taken for the purchase of these goods at normal prices were se't aside, and we all know how the prices soared and what enhanced prices we were obliged to pay ias compared with those that we would have paid had the suggestions and undertakings of the minister been carried out. In another place he says, along the same lines:-
All this action never cost Canada or Great Britain one dollar. Further, had the options on goods in the ealier part of the war been accepted at the time I had recommended the Committee, the saving to the British Government in the first six months of the war alone, would have been upwards of one hundred million of dollars.
That is a pretty concise statement made by a responsible minister -of the Crown at that time, and he charges this Government, those having the responsibility of conducting the purchases on behalf of the British Government in this country, he charges against them, without any equivocation, that had these recommendations been carried, out, and had the 'goods and supplies been furnished on the options he had obtained in the interest of the people generally, the British Government would have been saved in the first six months of the war upwards of one hundred million dollars. Then our hon. friends opposite hold up their hands in holy horror and shed tears because we o.n this side-of the House take the opportunity of bringing these matters to the attention of the Government and to the people, through the avenue of this forum where these matters are properly discussed. I say that no member of the Opposition has ever made so
strong a statement in regard to the weakness and the recklessness of the Administration who had charge of the purchase of supplies, as is made by the ex-minister himself. He says:
Let us now turn to another aspect. At the outbreak of the war, as I have stated, Canada had practically been brcmifht to the verge of bankruptcy.
Now hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House during this debate have charged that at the time of the defeat of the Liberal Government in 1911 Canada was on the verge of bankruptcy, and one hon. gentleman opposite said something like this: But the good Lord stepped in and intervened just in time to save Canada from bankruptcy. If the defeat of the Liberal Government in 1911 was the result of the intervention of the great Creator, then that old-fashioned Methodist hymn appeals to me more strongly than ever: "God moves in a mysterious way, his wonders to perform." If the Lord intervened in this case and put my hon, friends opposite in possession of the treasury benches to save the country from bankruptcy, then I want to ask my hon. friends opposite what answer they make to the charge of their colleague, their ' supporter, the gentleman with whom they have lived for so many years and have worked with hand in hand. He says:
At the outbreak of this war Canada bad practically been brought to the verge of bankruptcy, and my fear then was that we would not be able to maintain more than one division in the firing line.
Because why? Because we had not the money to supply other divisions. On the verge of bankruptcy ! We had not the money to supply the men, to supply the divisions* according to the hon. gentleman. He says further:
I had on two previous occasions pointedly drawn the Finance Minister's attention to the fact that his function was to produce a revenue, keep the business of the country buoyant, and thus, everything being prosperous, money would be easily obtainable. In this, however, success did not attend his efforts; or, rather, my suggestions were not accepted by that gentleman.
The hon. gentleman goes on and gives his warning. He speaks of the Nationalist party and the sorrow it gives him to have to offer these criticisms of the record of his own friends. Hon. gentlemen opposite as well as hon. members on this side of the House have, during this debate, as in all other debates in this House, referred, and properly so, to the responsibility rest-

ing upon Canada as part of the British Empire in the conduct of this war.
I do not know any better slogan that can be adopted in Canada than one which is now being used more or less throughout the country, and that is: "Win the war.'" I understand that during this month delegates from all o^Si. Canada will hold a win-the-war meeting in the city of Montreal. I do not for one moment insinuate, as our friends opposite do, that there are disloyal men in this House, on either side of the Speaker's chair. I do not want to say to hon. gentlemen opposite that they are not doing the best they can. While some people in the country may not have done as much as they might have done, I believe that the feeling uppermost in the mind of every loyal Canadian is that of willingness to do his best to assist in winning the war. But while the people can do their part; while individual members of Parliament can do their share, yet the lead must be taken and the trail blazed by the gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches, because only by them and through them can the country's efforts be best directed to assisting the Allies in this great conflict. I have said that there are three great elements entering into our participation in the war: we must have men, we must have money, and we must have munitions and supplies. Hon. gentlemen upon whom rests the responsibility for the conduct of our part in the war must come to Parliament and get money for that purpose. I want to ask hon. gentlemen opposite if they can offer one word of criticism against hon. gentlemen on this side in that they have refused ^to vote any of the money asked for by the Government in connection with Canada's part in the war. I have yet to learn, Sir, that any such criticism could successfully be made against the attitude of the Opposition in this respect since the outbreak of the war. Money has been voted in three sessions of Parliament; in the session which is now proceeding, part of the supply has already been voted. The burden rests upon the shoulders of the Government to spend every dollar of that money economically and in the best interests of the people of Canada and especially of those who are engaged in the war. We are not here to offer carping criticism in regard to small matters, but the financing of the war is a serious responsibility, and those who have charge of the expenditure of the money voted by Parliament should see to it -that every 
single dollar goes into the proper channel and is devoted to serving the best interests of the people. If the statements made by the ex-'M.inister of Militia and Defence, extracts from which I have Tead, are correct, a serious condition is revealed. He charges that in tlhe first six months of the war alone, hon. gentlemen opposite wasted $100,000,000 of the money of the British Government. When we see that hon. gentlemen opposite are unable to woik together in the interest of the whole country; when we see that they have thrown away in six months $100,000,000 of British money, is there not fair ground for the suspicion that money that has been taken from the people by way of taxation has been wasted? We know from investigations held, evidence adduced and findings made in different parts of Canada-I speak more particularly of my own province and the Maritime Provinces-that money has been wasted; that money has been taken from the proper channels and been diverted to the pockets of middlemen who had no business to act in that capacity. Not a few paltry dollars, Sir, but hundreds of thousands of dollars have gone into improper channels, and, this being the case, it is the duty of every hon. gentleman to bring the matter to the attention of the public. We do this not because we desire to 'embarrass the Government, but because we believe it is our duty to serve the best interests of the people who sent us here and who have not the opportunity of coming here and discussing it themselves. We in this House are only saying in a mild way what the people of the country generally have been saying in regard to the wasteful and extravagant expenditure that is going on. Should we be any more subject to the criticism of hon. gentlemen opposite for discussing these matters than the public press? You can scarcely pick up a newspaper which does not contain criticism of the Government and articles pointing out the blunders and mistakes made by hon. gentlemen opposite. Not only newspapers friendly to the Opposition, but newspapers friendly to the Administration are offering criticisms and making suggestions with the idea not of embarrassing the Government, .but of bringing about efficient administration and serving the best interests of the people generally. Newspapers are finding fault with the Government; individuals are writing thousands of letters in regard to these matters; yet we are charged with being disloyal because we

bring the attention of Parliament to them.
Why, Sir, we have charges of extravagance made in our municipal and town councils, and not only that, we have them from the pulpits. During the past year it was rather a miracle if when one of us went to a divine service on a Sunday morning, the minister did not preach a sermon against graft, wastefulness and extravagance, and single out the very men who had been feeding at the Government trough during the past five years and becoming rich at the expense of this country on war contracts; yet, we as members of Parliament, are told that we should come here and having eyes that see not and ears that hear not, and, to go a little further, voices that speak not, because forsooth, something might drop that might cause some embarrassment to the Government in doing their part in the conduct of this war.
We have given the Government money and they must accept the responsibility for the proper expenditure of it. The next question is with regard to the men. When the war first broke out, and the first call was made, a large number of our heroic young men immediately volunteered for service abroad and were at once hurried to Valcartier where they were placed in training camps in order to prepare for their duties in the field. I do not want to detract any of the credit that is due to the Government or due to the Minister of Militia at that time for the part they took in getting those men in training ready to go to the front. The first contingent sailed in the latter part of September, 1914. After these men had gone, others were enlisting; recruits were being asked fox and thousands were being hurried forward to do their parts. Finally recruiting officers were appointed in different parts of Canada; recruiting meetings were held, .and recruits were asked for to step into the ranks and enter training camps in order to fit themselves for service at the front. Shortly after that, a hundred thousand men were asked fox, then up to two hundred thousand men, then up to two hundred and fifty thousand men, and finally, I believe, on the 1st of February, 1916, the Premier of the Dominion promised that Canada would isupply 500,000 men. Unfortunately for Canada, unfortunately for the Empire, and more unfortunately still for the Canadians who are already at the front doing their part, the enlistments have not yet reached that total. I sincerely trust that some action will be taken by which the young
men of our country may be induced to realize what is their duty in defence of their country and in recognition of what our boys have already done, and go to the front to fill the gaps that are unfortunately too often occurring. All who have gone across the water to fight the battles of the Empire are of the best blood of Canada^, and wherever we have had any report of any engagements in which our Canadian boys have taken part nothing but the very best word has been received of their
12 p.m. valour. We know of the grand stand they have made in different places, and last, but not least, of the magnificent stand they are. making now at Vimy Ridge, where the fight has been raging for so many days, and where so many of our boys are falling. The casualty lists are large and let us hope that many young men in this country will come forward and fill the gaps. We sincerely trust that the Government will take some action in the matter, and I am sure I am voicing the sentiment of every hon. gentleman on this side of the House that anything we can do to assist the Government in recruiting and assist the Empire in winning this war we have always been prepared to do if the Government are prepared to take the responsibility of doing their part.
Even after we have the men, men are absolutely useless at the front unless they have munitions and supplies of, food and clothing. Here is where an opportunity occurs for the Government to do the noble thing, the grand thing, the big thing, and to hand this matter over to a commission, which will be prepared to make the necessary purchases in the interest of the country and not in the interest of a few profiteers. During the time this war has been going on, and where purchases have been made in the different parts of Canada, there has not been exercised that care that is becoming to the ordinary capable business man who would see to it that he purchased the necessary supplies in the economical way that we believe was the duty that this Government owed to the people of Canada. We have been accused of disloyalty; we have been accused of wasting time; we have been accused of not doing our duty in regard to recruiting and other matters in connection with the war; but fortunately for this side of the House we have one loyal man left, and that is my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark). Hon. gentlemen opposite always pay him the very high compliment of putting him almost on the same high pedestal

and plane in which they place themselves in regard to the conduct of the war. They went so far the other day, I 'believe, as to offer an invitation tto my hon. friend to come over, saying that he would be more happy with them than he would 'be with us. In fact, they prepared a chair trimmed with fine purple and gold lace and urged the hon. gentleman to come over and occupy it. I can imagine my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and my hon. friend the member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames), the archangels of protection, leading my hon. friend, the archangel of free trade, over to the other side of the House to hobnob with them in regard to the conduct of the war. We are glad to know that we have on this side of the House one man who appeals to the loyalty and the good feeling of my hon. friends opposite. While we respect the hon. gentleman's opinions in regard to this war, I do not think there is a gentleman on this side of the House but is just as loyal, has just as much sympathy and just as much desire to see the Allies win this war as our very eminent colleague on this side whom we all respect.
There has been a good deal of criticism in the newspapers, because recruiting has been slow, and many reasons have been given for that condition of affairs. One reason is that it is due to the extravagance of the Government, but I think one of the strongest reasons that can be urged as a cause of the slow recruiting in the Dominion of Canada is because throughout every province where recruiting meetings have been held, where officers have been appointed, where Supplies have been purchased, everything that has been done in connection with the enlisting, training and equipping of our soldiers has been conducted along a purely political patronage arrangement, and the people in the various provinces have come to realize that they are not being properly treated, because they feel that the war and the expenditure in connection with it should be carried on without this political patronage.
But even at this late date I believe that if the Government were big enough to do their part our young men would come forward by the thousands and fill up the gaps in the ranks. Why does not the Government follow the preachments of the Minister of Trade and Commerce? That hon. gentleman was very eloquent last session and again this session on the subject of political patronage, and I really believe he

meant what he said at the time. "Political patronage," he said, "I hate it." Yet in spite of the influence one would think he	would	have	with	his	colleagues,the	same	thing	goes	on	day after
day and week after week and year after year. Only a few days ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a statement in the House in regard to the high cost of living. He said that we must produce more, and save more. As this is the hon. gentleman's opinion, I would ask him first of all to have a heart to heart talk with the Minister of Finance, pointing out to him his duty under present conditions. Then let him have a talk with the Minister of Militia and every other member of the Government. We always listen to the hon. gentleman with a very great deal of pleasure, but when this Government does not act up to his preaching, when we realize that his words are simply words and nothing more, we may well doubt whether this Government intends to do any better in the future. The Minister of Trade and Commerce took the right attitude in regard to production and still more production, the necessity for thrift, and the avoidance of waste. It is, of course, the farmers of this country that we must look to for greater production. What encouragement, I should like to know, is this Government giving to agriculture at the present time? We have heard a great deal about the farmers of the West, but very little is said of the farmers of the East. At last, after many years, and in spite of the arguments practically throughout the whole history of the Conservative party that it would be suicidal to this country to open up trade avenues with the great republic to the south, in spite of their determination to have no truck or trade with the Yankees, they have at last granted facilities- for the free interchange of wheat and wheat products between this country and the United States. Wheat, of course, is grown largely in the West, but a large number of farm products are also produced in the Maritime Provinces and in Quebec, and our people would have been glad to see the Government go a little further -in. this matter of free trade with the United States, and give our farmers in the East free bran and shorts to feed their cattle. They would have liked to see the Government give them cheaper feed for their dairy cows, and then we would not have to pay 50 cents a pound for 'butter. A great deal has been said about the high prices

the farmers are getting, 'but it is a fallacy to suppose that they are reaping much extra benefit from the present high prices of farm products. Practically the only farmers who are reaping any benefit at the present time are those who were fortunate enough to have a fairly good supply on hand when prices began to soar. For instance, a man with a 'barn full of cattle a year ago would certainly profit by the present high prices, but when he wants to replenish his bam he has to pay a high price himself for his young cattle, and for their feed, and consequently on this second lot he will be making no more profit than in ordinary times, and the same thing is true in regard to .other products of the farm. A man who is getting 40 cents for his eggs is really no better off than he was a year ago when he was getting 25 cents. The high prices for farm products are discounted by reason of the fact that it takes more money to buy feed and flour and all the other commodities that the farmer needs.
A great deal has been said in this H.ouse on the high cost of living; we had a debate on that subject only the other day. The hon. member for West Lamibton (Mr. Pardee) has referred to the remarks of the Minister of Labour on that subject this afternoon. The Minister of Lab,our would have us believe that the Government have seized every opportunity to bring down the high cost of living. Judging from the minister's remarks, he has been very busy looking into these matters. With the exception of a short recess we have been sitting here continuously from January, and there has been haTdly a day in all that time when the necessaries of life have not been rising at an enormous rate. Only the other day flour went up by $1.20 a barrel, and that was rather a staggering blow for hon. gentlemen in this House, and for the people of this country.
Some hon. members on this side asked the Minister of Labour what action had been taken. It then appeared that a jump cf $1.20 a barrel in the price of flour in one day had awakened the minister from his slumbers, and that he had taken action. He stated that he had grappled with the situation and had done all that could be done. And what action had he taken? He had sent Mr. O'Connor to Montreal to inquire into the cause. And Mr. O'Connor must have done good service, foT the next day the price of flour went up sixty cents more. The Minister of Labour took a great deal of time to explain what he had done- It
appears that he has received reports and has had these tabulated, and that a great deal of other work has been done in the department. But while this has been going on the prices of the necessaries of life have been advancing and are advancing to-day, and we are getting beyond what is reasonable and beyond what the ordinary people can afford. When it was suggested by my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) and others on this side that we should commandeer wheat, or commandeer the flour mills, or take some either action, what was the reply of the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White)? That hon. gentleman figured out that there was in Canada 100,000,(XX) bushels of wheat and that if we commandeered this at $3 a bushel, three hundred millions of money would be required in order to take charge of it. Does the Minister of Finance really think that the people can be hoodwinked and! fooled in this way? It does not require the raising of $300,000,000 to commandeer wheat for the people. All the minister iwould need to do is to repeat what he did in regard to newsprint paper, or what the Minister of Labour said he had done when certain railway corporations refused to accept the finding of the board of conciliation. In this latter case the Minister of Labour simply said to these people:	You will be coming to this Government and asking for privileges some of these days, and unless you pay the men the wages reported by the board, you will not get any privileges. If the Minister of Finance should go to his friends the millers and to. his friends who control commodities in this country, and tell them that unless certain things were done he would take action, that action would never need to be taken. These people would simply do what they believe to be in the interests of the country, as led and directed by the minister.
I have said that the prices of the foods that arc required on the table of both rich and poor alike are going beyond what is reasonable. It is very well for us who, possibly, are in such circumstances as to be able to supply our tables with all we want irrespective of the high prices, to gather here and offer our tribute of sympathy to those who are less fortunate. But let me tell the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour, who give such loud assurances that the people of Canada were never so well off as they are to-day, that, while they may represent the condition of affairs existing in their own constituencies

or in those sections of the country which they know best, they are not setting forth the condition of affairs' existing in many of the counties, towns, and villages known to me and in which I have been within the past year. The unskilled labourers, the men who have to go out with pick and shovel to earn a livelihood, are not getting a full supply of even the necessaries of life to-day. I do not charge the Government with bringing about this condition, but I say that this condition exists-that many wage-earners are not receiving enough to furnish their tables with the food neces-saray for their families. And, this being so, something should be done if it is at all possible. The Minister of Labour tells us that he is keeping tab on the coal dealers of St. John and of Montreal. But I do not need to ask the Minister of Labour when I need certain information with regard to food prices and the causes of inflated value. Go to the grocery store or to the market, right here in the city of Ottawa, and ask why eggs are at their present price. You will at once receive the information that eggs are being bought up by gentlemen who are putting them away in cold storage with a view of enhancing the prices and making the people pay more than eggs are worth. And what is happening in regard to eggs is happening in regard to other food products. The people of this country must have that which will keep body and soul together. And when the Minister of Labour says wages are high in this country, he is probably referring to the wages of skilled labour. It is true that in the manufacture of munitions and in other skilled employments high wages are paid. But the wages paid to the common labourer are not sufficient to enable him to meet the rise in the prices of foodstuffs. The $1.50 or $1.75 a day that the ordinary labourer used to receive three years ago, had greater purchasing power than the $2 or $2.50 he receives to-day. And, while I sympathize with anybody who has to pay extortionate or extravagant prices for the food or clothes required for his family, yet I realize that the man with the high salary can afford it, and does not need much sympathy. When flour could be bought at $5 and $6 a barrel, the labourers could get along very well without much meat, for flour was a cheap food for the family table of the poor man. That is past and gone, and it is the duty of the Government, of the Labour Department and of all concerned, to make any 
suggestions that will assist the ordinary man to get along better on what he has and to live happily and in a more contented Way.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance brought down his Budget the other day in a few well chosen words, and wound up by telling us that the country was very prosperous. He proved beyond peradventure that the country was prosperous because of the war. Trade and revenue had improved, and we were better off to-day than we were in 1913. If Canada is better off to-day than in 1913, she can only be better off because of the war. Therefore, if we want prosperity, I suppose it is better to have the war continue as long as possible; that would be the logical conclusion one must come to from the reasoning of hon. gentlemen opposite. We take the hon. gentleman's statement, and we find that in 1913 the revenue was only $130,000,000. That increased a little in 1914, and it increased again last year, when the revenue amounted to $232,000,000. That is a wonderful increase in revenue, and therefore the country is prosperous. I am glad to know that Canada is getting on so well from the financial standpoint, and that she has been able to finance this war. But I would draw the attention of the minister to the fact that this increase in revenue and trade represent an illegitimate prosperity, and one that cannot be permanent. Very soon after the close of war we must get back, not only to where we were, but very much below where we were when the war broke out, because trade will be dislocated, and we will be undergoing a very rapid and necessary change. Under these conditions I do not think we have very much to be thankful for. He says that while we have spent $172,000,000 on ordinary and capital account we have the large and magnificent sum pf $60,000,000 to devote to war expenditure. Hon. members on this side of the House have, during the last two or three years, and especially when the estimates have been under consideration, tried to point out to hon. gentlmen 'opposite that it was their duty to curtail and stop unnecessary expenditure, to get down to hard pan, where the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) would have us if we would judge by his remarks and his estimates. We should keep the expenditure down to as low a point as possible. I find that in 1911 we only spent $118,000,000 on ordinary and capital account. Just previous to the war, when our revenues were

buoyant and everything was prosperous, the Government spent $118,000,000. Last year, when the war was at its very worst, when everything was looking black and everybody interested in the outcome was advising economy, this economical Government, this Government that preaches economy and practices extravagance, spent $172,000,000 on ordinary and capital account. Now it takes great credit that it was able to apply $60,000,000 to the war expenditure. As was so well pointed out by my hon. friend from Northumberland, the extra taxation that they placed upon the people last year more than made up the $60,000,000, and that amount that they have taken credit for having applied to the war expenditure was simply taken out of the poor people of this country. I do not say that the war expenditure should not come out of the people because there is no other source from which ' it can come. But a very serious question arises and it is as to how much of this money should be provided by increasing customs duties and how much should be taken from the people by direct taxation. The	Minister of	Finance	takes a
very	great deal of credit because
the loans that he has asked for have been over-subscribed. When he asked for $100,000,000 he got $150,000,000, and when he asked for $200,000,000 he got $100,000,000 more than he asked for. That is all very well, and it speaks well for the patriotism of the people but men who have money lying in the savings bank drawing three per cent, when they have an opportunity of handing it over and taking securities from the Government at 5i and 6 per cent, naturally come forward and take up these bonds. I am not casting the slightest reflection upon the people that do that, but it is a very easy thing to be patriotic when you are being paid well for it. In my opinion there is an opportunity to find out where the money is and where the millionaires are. The banks took up a large part of the first loan but the banks were not allowed to take any of the last loan, although they were willing to take $60,000,000 of it. We have had to raise $600,000,000 for the carrying on of this war. We are told by the Minister of Finance that we will have to raise at least $600,000,000 more. The question that arises in the mind of every business man in this; Is it a proper thing to borrow all this money and extend the repayment of it over a long term of years, or will it be a proper thing to finance some of this war out of a present levy of taxation
upon the people. I contend that under the present arrangement when we are gathering in a large part of the revenue from the customs tariff, we are faking more than a proper share out of the poor men of the country. The Minister of Finance said that the question of taxing incomes and taxing wealth has been considered by the Government and that because of the fact that there is very little concentration of wealth in the Dominion they thought that it would not be a wise thing to tax wealth. I for one believe that the greater part of the financial burden of this war should be carried by the wealth of this country. While my hon. friend says that by the business war tax he is placing an impost upon the wealth of the country, to my mind he is not placing it altogether where it should be placed and gathering the revenue from the people who are best able to pay. The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) tonight showed by two or three very apt illustrations how unfairly this taxation falls on different individuals. I would not go so far as to say that we should pay the whole costs of the war by direct taxation, but I do think that we should be paying more than $60,000,000 per annum. If the Government had expended last year only what the old Government had expended in its last year of office, then out of the revenue which this Government raised of $232,000,000, they would have had something over $100,000,000 to apply to the expenses of the war. But they did not do that, and now they have borrowed the greater part of the money required for carrying on the war. I do contend that in a crisis such as this the wealth of our country should contribute more than it has contributed up to the present time. The Minister of Finance says that it will be well enough to tax incomes when we get to the length of our tether and have not any other revenue; then he says we will tax the income of the rich man. Let me remind my hon. friend that when this war is over and business is dull, when things are not going as they are to-day, when we are beginning to dismantle the munition plants,, when munition (workers who have been, working at high salaries for the last two years are thrown back on our hands, when the soldiers are returning maimed and wounded and in need of a great deal of money to assist them, then will not be an opportune time to impose the extra taxation. Now is the time, when money is plentiful, when, our friends are getting on well and making money, not only out of their

regular business but out of the manufacture of munitions of war. I would offer a slight criticism in regard to my hon. friend's mode of extra taxation. I think he should distinguish between taxation on regular business profits and profits made from the manufacture of munitions. The reason for that, to my mind, is that the ordinary business man, who has been in business, possibly as a corporation, for years, has had his lean years, has had his hard times, has had his struggle; he has had to work day and night to build up a trade, and possibly now he has got a very good business established and is making a good return on his investment. That is all very well, let him pay a certain tax on his profit. But the man who is making big profits out of the manufacture of munitions is in a different position. He has been practically financed from the beginning by the Government. He has had no financial struggle or difficulty, as his machinery was provided by the excessive prices paid him by the Government for their first order of munitions, as was abundantly proved in this House, and as is known to every man familiar with the subject. I say that a very much higher tax should be placed on the profits made from munition work than on ordinary business profits. While I grant that the ordinary business has profited to a certain extent and been encouraged because of the war, it has not been encouraged nearly so much, nor has it received so much assistance from the Government, as the munition workers, who have been making great profits.
I wish to speak briefly upon the operations of the Intercolonial railway. That is a subject that is very dear to all men from the Maritime Provinces, and, according to hon. gentlemen opposite, the people from Ontario and the West, who have now a part of the Intercolonial, claim that it is no longer a child of ours, and is therefore interesting to the whole people of Canada. I am glad hon. gentlemen are taking such an active interest in the Intercolonial in our part of the country. As to the credit which is to be taken for the operation of the Intercolonial in the past year, ,there may be some difference of opinion. Hon. gentlemen opposite claim that credit because the road has earned almost double the revenue of past years. That is very easily explained. It is not because the operation of the Intercolonial has been of a particularly business-like 
character. The increased revenue results from the raising of the tariff rates and freight rates. Then, during the last year the Intercolonial earned large amounts of money by the transport of munitions and troops. These services have been charged for at the highest prices, and the money to pay for them has been borrowed by the Government. That is why the Intercolonial has earned such a large income during the past year.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) is very interesting to members on this side of the House. We have always followed that line, we have always aimed to get as near as possible to free trade, and we congratulate the Government very heartily, indeed, for at last having had their eyes opened and having come to the realization that the farmers of the West must have this free interchange of wheat and wheat products between Canada and the United States. I hope it is permanent. Some question has been raised and very fine legal points have been argued by hon. gentlemen who have addressed the House. I sincerely trust that the opinion given on this matter by the Deputy Minister of Justice is correct, and that the arrangement is permanent and will be lasting.
It is evident that there is a doubt in the minds of eminent lawyers as to whether the Deputy Minister of Justice is correct in his view, but, whether he is correct or not, we want to make sure that this provision of free wheat shall be a permanent arrangement. Under the circumstances, therefore, the Government should accept the amendment of the hon. member for Assiniboia and thereby make it plain to the people that this arrangement* is a permanent one, that there shall be no more tinkering with this part of the tariff and that there shall be free exchange of wheat and wheat products between Canada and the United States. We sincerely hope that this will be the thin edge of the wedge; that more products will be placed on the free list and that there shall be a freer exchange of commodities between the two countries. As a matter of fact, we hope that we shall get what -we should have had in 1911, reciprocity with the United States, which would be beneficial to them and beneficial to the people of Canada generally because of the resulting increase of trade.
The House divided on the amendment of Mr. Turriff.

maintopic: M. VIVIANI TO ADDRESS CANADIAN PARLIAMENT.
M. VIVIANI TO ADDRESS CANADIAN PARLIAMENT.
speechtext:
Before the House adjourns,
I wish to make a short announcement, after consultation with my right hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition. Two very important missions from Europe have been in the United States for the last fortnight, one representing the British Government and the other the French Republic. Both of those Commissions have been invited to make at least a short visit to Canada as the guests of the Government and of the people. We have to remember the very honourable and responsible position held by the members of both missions, representing their respective countries as _ the guests of the Government and people of the United States who had the first call on their time. The members of those missions, however, have been very anxious if they could find it at all possible to visit Canada. The time set for the French mission was much shorter than that set for the British mission and they are obliged to leave at a certain fixed date. I am, however, very happy tc be able to announce that the French mission will make Canada a short visit, necessarily very short, but none the less hearty and sincere that it is short, and that on Saturday we shall have in Ottawa for a few hours M. Viviani, the former premier, and at present the Minister of Justice of the French Government. He will, whilst here, make the acquaintance of members of both Houses. M. Viviani, who is a most noted speaker and orator, has addressed both Houses of the Congress of the United States and he has consented to address both Houses of this Parliament. With
the consent of the House, I shall ask to-
%

morrow night that instead of adjourning we shall suspend the sitting, with the understanding that Mr. Speaker will take the Chair at twelve o'clock noon on Saturday, about which hour M. Viviani will be present and will deliver an address to both Houses of Parliament.
With reference to Marshall Joffre, it is impossible for him to come to Ottawa, but he will be able to visit Montreal on Sunday of next week, also as the guest of the Government. We all feel the very great honour of a visit from these gentlemen and I am sure that our reception of them will be most cordial. That they have not been able to make a longer stay with us is due to the imminence of their departure and their pressing duties. I may say that later on we shall have a visit to Canada of the British mission headed by the Right Hon. A. J. Balfour.

maintopic: M. VIVIANI TO ADDRESS CANADIAN PARLIAMENT.
speechtext:
The announcement which has just been made by my right hon. friend will certainly he most welcome to all Canada. There would, indeed, have been great disappointment if the French and the British delegation had not visited our country, and I am sure that my right hon. friend has voiced the sentiments of this House in particular in stating that on Saturday at 12 o'clock we shall have the privilege of hearing M. Viviani, the chief of the French delegation. I am glad that my right hon. friend has made this announcement, because it will be made public to-morrow, and I am sure that in consequence we shall have a very large attendance.
On motion of Sir George Foster the House adj.ourned at 1.20 a.m. Friday.
